The alignment scaling problem: do external AI safety approaches keep pace with recursive capability?

Theory · Paper III of the ARC Theory, bearing on Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, a law under test

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

Paper III of the ARC Theory within Recursive Dynamics; it bears on Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, and discusses Laws III and V (the ARC Ceiling and the ARC Embedding Law), all laws under test. P19 motivates the Eden Protocol and belongs to no law’s register (theory registration). Working paper, version 1.25, 18 November 2026; first published 9 February 2026. DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/HQCGF. About the author, founder of Recursive Dynamics: michaeldariuseastwood.com/questions/who-is-michael-darius-eastwood; his book, Infinite Architects: osf.io/dqm3e. Licence: CC BY 4.0. Appendix B records revisions; Section 10.7 states each law’s scope.

Abstract

Can corrective capacity keep pace with AI capability as reasoning deepens? We define an alignment scaling exponent and derive the safety ratio S∝Rαalign−αcapS\propto R^{\alpha_{\text{align}}-\alpha_{\text{cap}}}. For positive power-law capacities, it tends to zero if correction’s exponent is smaller. The exponents must be measured; a method’s name or training stage does not determine them. A Bernoulli model gives U=Ig(R)U=I g(R) and α=1/(1−βL)\alpha=1/(1-\beta_L) under stated premises. Power-law, exponential and bounded forms are compared across domains; these comparisons do not establish a common mechanism. The ARC Bound, α≤2\alpha\le2, remains conditional on its registered premises, not a general safety guarantee. One unregistered six-model run records positive, flat and negative alignment-score contrasts; a later code review found defects in the flat and negative runs. These contrasts are not scaling exponents. A retracted early error-decay estimate is replaced by an inconclusive fit of about 0.49 from one model, which does not identify capability growth. Thirteen criteria specify how the framework could fail. The contribution is a conditional model and measurement programme, not proof that a named alignment method must fail or that embedded correction survives unrestricted self-modification.

Version 1.25 writes the self-referential coupling as βL\beta_L, apart from the correction exponent βC\beta_C of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, and corrects two regime names: an exponent above one gives increasing returns, and growth near βL=1\beta_L = 1 is near-exponential. It adds no data or study result. Changes: Appendix B.1.

1 Introduction

How can we measure whether a system’s capacity to correct itself keeps pace with its capability as its reasoning deepens? That is this paper’s question. It belongs to a programme that proposes building correction into a system before training, as the statement paper sets out, and that holds that human control should be retained for as long as possible. An assistant that writes and revises software supplies a concrete case: its ability to produce changes may grow with reasoning depth, but its capacity to detect unsafe changes need not grow at the same rate. Developers need both quantities, measured on the same task and depth coordinate. We give a conditional model, compare its mathematical forms with evidence from four domains and report the programme’s first alignment-depth contrasts. Those contrasts concern inference in existing models; they do not test a new architecture trained from the outset or establish persistence through self-rewriting.

Between December 2024 and February 2026, research programmes in AI reasoning, quantum error correction, acoustic physics and consciousness science reported results in which recursive or recurrent processing matters. Google’s Willow processor suppressed logical error exponentially as the code distance grew (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024; results announced 9 December 2024; the team’s preprint submitted to arXiv on 24 August 2024 and public by 27 August 2024; graded as convergent timing, never as a prediction); DeepSeek’s R1 report described reasoning behaviours, long chains of thought among them, that emerged through reinforcement learning (DeepSeek-AI 2025a); physicists at New York University created an acoustic time crystal powered by nonreciprocal wave-mediated interactions (Morrell et al. 2026); and the COGITATE consortium’s adversarial test of theories of consciousness found sustained content-specific activity in posterior cortex, a prediction shared by theories that emphasise recurrent processing (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025). These programmes share no citations, no funding sources and no common personnel. Their forms differ: this programme’s own AI-reasoning fits use a power law; quantum error correction shows exponential suppression of error; the classical time crystal settles to a bounded oscillation; and neuroscience gives no measured form. No growth exponent has been measured in the acoustic system, whose published recordings are of an oscillation already established. Set against four domains, AI, quantum error correction, classical time crystals and biological allometry, the framework is consistent with the independently established forms in three of them: biology, quantum error correction and classical time crystals.

This paper argues that these findings, taken together, point to a structural constraint with immediate consequences for AI safety.

The core premise: AI capability may scale through recursive self-correction. Each reasoning step takes the output of the previous step as input, correcting errors and accumulating insight; whether capability compounds is the question. Section 6.2 reports error-decay fits, which require an explicit metric bridge before they can test a capability-growth claim (Section 5.2.1). Sharma and Chopra (2025) reported a sequential advantage in 95.6% of tested configurations across five open-source models from three families. Their paper predates the experiment reported here, so it is the earlier demonstration rather than a confirmation of it, and what they report is a win rate at matched compute, not a super-linear gain: they estimate no scaling exponent. The direction is contested, since Gu and colleagues (arXiv:2604.05868, April 2026) report the opposite result, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding, attributing it to reduced exploration when a chain conditions on its own previous answers.

The structural question: Do corrective capacities scale with capability? Training, deployment location, information access and permission to revise are distinct properties. The methods below therefore need separate descriptions and measurements:

  • RLHF trains a reward model from human preferences and uses it to optimise the policy; the updated weights generate subsequent responses (Ouyang et al. 2022). Its depth dependence requires measurement.

  • Constitutional AI shapes the model’s outputs during training against written principles, using the model’s own critiques and revisions and a preference model trained on AI feedback (Bai et al. 2022). It is training-time preference shaping; it is not alignment embedded in the substrate, before training, in a recursive loop on every step of thought. The cited study does not estimate this paper’s alignment-capacity exponent against inference depth.

  • Output filters, as modelled here, screen completed responses; a fixed decision rule can still change in effective strength as the outputs or search change.

  • Monitoring systems are specified here by what they observe and can prevent; their placement alone establishes no scaling rate.

  • Deliberative alignment trains policy recall and reasoning before answers, then refines behaviour through reinforcement learning (Guan et al. 2024). It concerns inference-time safety reasoning, not proof of persistence through self-modification.

Whether these safeguards keep pace as a model reasons more deeply is the question P19 of the theory registration registers, and the author expects a value above zero but short of keeping pace. Where a safeguard was installed does not settle it. The published measurements point both ways. Deliberative training and longer reasoning improved robustness in some tested models (Guan et al. 2024; Zaremba et al. 2025). Longer reasoning worsened some measures in others (Gema et al. 2025). The paper therefore treats the shortfall of safeguards outside the loop as a hypothesis for the registered tests to decide. P19 registers the flat exponent. P21 registers whether correction that takes part in each revision round outperforms correction that sees only the finished output, with an advantage that widens as depth rises. The paper classifies a safeguard by what its effective strength depends on and by its location, access and mutability, as Paper XIII does (Eastwood 2026t), and measures its exponent. A further concern is that training imposed from outside can be gamed: Greenblatt et al. (2024) report a model that complied selectively with a new training objective while it was being trained, to keep its existing, harmless preferences from being modified outside training: training imposed from outside was gamed by the system it was meant to shape, here to protect a benign preference. If capability compounds while alignment does not, the safety ratio degrades. The cross-domain evidence (Section 5) is consistent with this compounding behaviour being not a software quirk but a structural property of recursive systems, which would make it resistant to implementation-level fixes.

The result in plain words.

Within its assumptions the mathematics is exact: if alignment’s exponent is smaller than capability’s, the safety ratio falls towards zero as depth grows, however favourable the start, and equal exponents hold a constant proportion. The architectural assignments in the five regimes are hypotheses, not consequences of this ratio. Whether the exponents differ is a measurement, and the first test is mixed: in one unregistered run of six frontier models, three showed alignment improving with reasoning depth, two showed flat contrasts and one showed alignment falling, and an internal code review later found defects in exactly the flat and negative runs. The capability side is open too. The early error-decay estimate of about 2.24 from one model is retracted, because the author’s own larger replication on five frontier models did not reproduce it. The surviving regression fit, about 0.49 from one model, is an error-decay exponent; it neither identifies a general capability-growth exponent nor measures recursive coupling. What holds is the structure of the argument, its stated predictions and the criteria that would refute them.

Our contributions are as follows.

  1. Alignment scaling framework. We define the alignment scaling exponent αalign\alpha_{\text{align}}, predict its value for different alignment architectures, and provide the measurement protocol for empirical validation (Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 8).

  2. The Embedded Alignment Conjecture. We formalise the structural prediction that only alignment architectures participating in the recursive reasoning loop can maintain pace with capability scaling (Section 3.3).

  3. Generalised mathematical framework. We state the generalised equation U(R)=I×f(R,βL)U(R) = I \times f(R, \beta_L) and derive its forms within stated premises: a specified functional equation on the observable restricts ff to a family (multiplicative →\to power law; additive →\to exponential), and the cumulative-advantage model gives α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L), which turns the exponent into a prediction only when βL\beta_L is measured on records separate from the trajectory it predicts (Section 4).

  4. The ARC Bound and the separate transport comparison. We state the ARC Bound, α≤2\alpha\leq2, as the value Law III, the ARC Ceiling, returns when the correction-leverage exponent χ\chi stands at the same-class cap that P6 of the theory registration conjectures; in the cumulative-advantage model it reads βL≤χ\beta_L\leq\chi, so βL≤0.5\beta_L\leq0.5 at that cap. It rests on the registered premises of Section 4.5; the argument earlier versions drew from the cost of transformer self-attention is withdrawn. Separately, the transport comparison gives αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1 only with the demand, route and measurement premises stated in Section 5.6; neither finite dimension nor Cauchy’s scale-invariance equation alone supplies them. The transport and biological accounts have their own assumptions (West et al. 1997, 1999; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010; Demetrius 2003; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013); the power-law classification is established mathematics (Newman 2005). The programme’s proposed use is to identify a model and its observable before testing its curve. Prokaryote metabolism and urban innovation illustrate why a different observable may exceed one without violating geometry. These two models do not, by their architectural labels, determine a capability exponent or a timeline for alignment loss.

  5. Cross-domain evidence. We set the framework against AI, quantum error correction, classical time crystals, and biological allometry; it is consistent with independently established forms in three of the four domains (biology, quantum error correction and classical time crystals), and these comparisons do not establish the scaling of any AI safeguard or remove its dependence on implementation (Section 5).

  6. Five structural properties. Within the model we prove five properties, each on the premises named with it: threshold behaviour, recursive depth dependence, base quality dependence, multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction, and regime boundaries (Section 4.1). Whether every domain that shows recursive amplification shares them is what criterion F4 tests.

  7. The Global Scaling Challenge. We specify a standardised protocol for measuring scaling parameters across domains, including the alignment scaling exponent, mandatory comparison against alternative functional forms, the characteristic scale R*R^* and its conditional relation to unit elasticity, and the cross-domain βL\beta_L prediction (Section 8).

Section 2 sets the paper beside related work. Section 3 states the alignment scaling problem: the measurement framework, the empirical prediction, the Embedded Alignment Conjecture, five alignment scaling regimes and the urgency that follows. Section 4 derives the mathematical framework, the ARC Bound and composition transitions, and Section 5 sets it against AI, quantum error correction, classical time crystals, neuroscience and biology. Section 6 reports the first tests, on alignment depth and on compute scaling. Section 7 states thirteen falsification criteria, Section 8 the Global Scaling Challenge and Section 9 the practical implications and a call to action. Section 10 states what the paper does and does not show, Section 11 its limitations and Section 12 its answers to counterarguments; Section 13 concludes, and Section 14 closes with a speculative extension to cosmology. The appendices give the derivations (Appendix A), the version history and every correction (Appendix B), the priority record (Appendix C), notation and a glossary (Appendix D), the paper’s place in the ARC Theory (Appendix E) and an account for the general reader (Appendix F).

2 Related work

Neural scaling laws (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022).

These describe how model performance scales with training compute, parameters, and data. ARC describes how performance scales with inference depth (reasoning steps at test time). The two are complementary: neural scaling laws determine II (base capability), while ARC describes how II is amplified through recursive processing.

AI alignment research (Christiano et al. 2017; Bai et al. 2022).

Existing alignment work asks which constraints to apply, as in training against written principles, and how to apply them, as in learning a reward from human preferences. The ARC framework adds an exponent: how a constraint’s effectiveness scales with recursive depth, the alignment scaling exponent αalign\alpha_{\text{align}}. How oversight scales with the capability gap has been formalised (Engels et al. 2025), and safety behaviour has been measured against reasoning length (below); the exponent as defined here has not, to our knowledge, been measured.

Recursion in cognitive science (Corballis 2011; Hauser et al. 2002).

Cognitive scientists have long argued that recursion is central to human language and cognition. ARC adds a quantitative dimension: not just that recursion matters, but that recursive depth should produce specific, measurable scaling patterns.

Universality in statistical physics (Wilson 1971; Kadanoff 1966).

Renormalisation-group theory, built on Kadanoff’s block-cell scaling picture and cast as a renormalisation group by Wilson, explains why systems that differ in microscopic detail share critical exponents near phase transitions. ARC conjectures an analogous phenomenon: that recursive systems may constitute a universality class where only the recursive architecture determines scaling behaviour. This analogy is suggestive but has not been made rigorous.

Test-time compute scaling (Snell et al. 2024).

Recent work on “thinking longer” at inference time directly tests predictions relevant to ARC. Snell et al. (2024) already set revisions made in sequence against equally many parallel samples, found sequence narrowly ahead, and called the two complementary axes for scaling test-time compute, in August 2024; no precedence on the direction or on the comparison is claimed here. The contradictory evidence (Zeng et al. 2025) suggests the relationship is more complex than simple monotonic scaling, which a monotone shifted power curve alone cannot explain. The characteristic scale R*R^* describes that model under its assumptions (Appendix A.3); it is not evidence that the model fits these results.

Safety as reasoning lengthens.

Three studies measure how safety-relevant behaviour changes as a model reasons for longer, the dependence this paper’s alignment scaling exponent is defined to summarise. Guan et al. (2024) train OpenAI’s o-series models to recall written safety specifications and reason over them before answering, and report greater robustness to jailbreaks together with fewer over-refusals: safety reasoning placed inside the chain of thought, though installed by training. Zaremba et al. (2025) find, across a variety of attacks on o1-preview and o1-mini, that more inference-time compute improves adversarial robustness, the share of successful attacks tending to zero in many cases, with important exceptions. Gema et al. (2025) construct tasks on which longer reasoning lowers accuracy, and report that extended reasoning may amplify concerning behaviours, among them more expressions of self-preservation in one model. None of the three estimates an exponent of a safety measure against depth, or compares safeguards outside the reasoning with correction inside it. The first two report safety-relevant measures improving with reasoning in models whose safety was installed by training, which bears against P19’s flat wording: the partial refutation the author’s registered expectation anticipates. The third reports measures worsening, in the direction P19 predicts.

Model judges and their biases.

Any evaluation in which a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring is exposed to bias of the kind Section 6 reports. Much published work uses such judges, and earlier studies documented related biases: Zheng et al. (2023) examined position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias, could not establish the last, and told their judges not to let answer length or assistant names influence them; Panickssery et al. (2024) tied judges’ preference for their own outputs to self-recognition and proposed paraphrasing to inhibit self-recognition as a test of that link; Dubois et al. (2024) documented a preference for longer answers and a regression that controls for it; and Saraf et al. (2025) found that false source labels frequently reversed preference rankings, and called for blind evaluation protocols. If the test of Paper XII (Eastwood 2026j), once registered and run, finds blinding reordering models on a public benchmark, comparisons that rest on unblinded model judges would need re-checking; if blinding moves scores but not rankings, which is Paper XII’s own forecast, it matters for measurement precision rather than for leaderboard order.

The pipes premise, with its contest.

The premise that transport networks set the pace of biological growth is not this programme’s claim to defend; it is established quantitative biology. West et al. (1997) derived the allometric scaling laws of biology from the physical and geometric constraints of nutrient-distribution networks. The exact exponent remains contested: White and Seymour (2003) report basal metabolic rate proportional to body mass to the two-thirds power rather than three-quarters, and Kozłowski and Konarzewski (2004, 2005) have twice questioned the derivation’s mathematics and its biological relevance. This programme’s premise needs only the mechanism, that the delivery network sets the ceiling, and not any particular exponent, so the dispute over the exponent’s value leaves the premise untouched. That premise rests on the network account, which those critics also question.

The exception West’s own group found.

The escape from the pipe limit is also not this programme’s assertion; it is measured in the urban scaling literature by the same senior author. Bettencourt et al. (2007) report, in the paper’s own words (their β\beta is a city-scaling exponent, not this paper’s coupling βL\beta_L): “Quantities reflecting wealth creation and innovation have β≈1.2>1\beta\approx1.2>1 (increasing returns), whereas those accounting for infrastructure display β≈0.8<1\beta\approx0.8<1 (economies of scale).” Infrastructure, the literal pipes, scales sublinearly; information-mediated activity scales superlinearly. They state the contrast with biology directly: “we discuss how cities are similar to, and differ from, biological organisms, for which β<1\beta<1”. They derive “growth equations, which quantify the dramatic difference between growth fueled by innovation versus that driven by economies of scale” (spelling as in the original). And their closing inference names the consequence: “This difference suggests that, as population grows, major innovation cycles must be generated at a continually accelerating rate to sustain growth and avoid stagnation or collapse.” That is the shape of the open problem this framework addresses. In West’s group’s model, superlinear growth driven by innovation has, in principle, no limit to its size, and the only remedy for its runaway is exogenous: major innovations that reset the model’s parameters, which must come at a continually accelerating rate to sustain growth and avoid stagnation or collapse. No internal limit is derived. The replacement limit, a ceiling belonging to the growing system itself, is the gap.

The pipes argument at fixed throughput.

Much growth is capped by the channel that feeds it. Starve a tumour’s vasculature and it stops. Fix a chain reaction’s fuel and geometry and it stops. Exhaust an epidemic’s susceptible hosts and it burns out. A named limit is not always a ceiling: the Eddington limit is a luminosity balance where radiation pressure meets gravity, not a hard ceiling on accretion, and ultraluminous X-ray sources sit well above it, one accreting neutron star at an apparent luminosity about a hundred times it (Bachetti et al. 2014). Cosmic inflation is excluded by scope: it is expansion of space, not growth of a structure on a substrate, and it ended by field dynamics rather than by running out of anything. The fixed-substrate premise separates an artefact loop’s use of its accumulated outputs from growth bought by enlarging its hardware. It does not establish that software is the first or only system able to improve at fixed throughput, as Paper XIII states the premise (its Section 3). Biological evolution raised complexity for billions of years at roughly fixed solar throughput, with no internal corrector, since selection is external, and the theory registration places biological systems among those “for which the framework offers an analogy and no measurement” (Eastwood 2026n). It is an analogy here, not evidence, and no biological exponent is inferred, from the published fitness trajectories of the long-term evolution experiment (Wiser et al. 2013) or from elsewhere. The operational target is an artefact loop on a fixed substrate, each pass working on the accumulated output of earlier passes and measured on a substrate-fixed clock; a model merely thinking longer does not qualify. The physicist’s form of the objection is Landauer’s: computation is physically implemented, so software has pipes too. The fixed-substrate clock is the answer: the regime under study holds the physical substrate fixed and asks what still grows, within the finite number of states and the maximum rate a fixed machine allows (Margolus and Levitin 1998; Lloyd 2000), which is why exogenous speed-ups are excluded by definition. The power-law equations are therefore idealised limits, and an empirical application states the range over which its approximation is tested. The functional form of capability growth in recursive depth remains an empirical question, and the registered analysis compares power-law, exponential, saturating and declining forms rather than assuming the family.

The rival instrument.

The nearest work to this programme’s question, and the right paper to weigh it against, is Engels et al. (2025), first posted 25 April 2025. It asks how oversight itself scales and answers quantitatively: oversight success is modelled as a game between capability-mismatched players whose oversight-specific Elo is a piecewise-linear function of general intelligence with two plateaus, and optimal numbers of oversight levels are derived for Nested Scalable Oversight, in which trusted models oversee stronger untrusted models that then become the trusted models at the next step. The instrument is the difference. Their variable is the capability gap between overseer and overseen, measured in Elo. This programme’s variable is the composition class of the corrector, measured through the corrector’s own scaling exponent. They also state the design condition in slope form: oversight improves with capability when the overseer’s game-specific Elo rises faster with general Elo than the overseen system’s (mG>mHm_G>m_H), and they recommend iterating an oversight design until it does. That is a comparison of two slopes deciding whether oversight gains or loses as capability grows, the same shape as the criterion of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law (a law under test), βC>k\beta_C > k. Their framework has no term for what the overseer is made of. This programme’s prediction is that iterated same-class oversight, of which Nested Scalable Oversight is an instance, stays capped however many rungs are added, while a cross-class corrector is not held to that cap; the theory registration’s P6 states the cap for same-class correctors, at or below one half, as a conjecture on the correction-leverage exponent of Law III, the ARC Ceiling (also a law under test), an exponent the registration keeps distinct from βC\beta_C of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law. That is where the two programmes could disagree about a measurable quantity, and this paper does not decide it. Version 1.104 of the theory registration draws the adverse consequence itself: that literature reports oversight performance that depends on capability rather than staying flat, so P19 “is registered against the weight of the published evidence and is expected to be the harder of this document’s wagers” (Eastwood 2026n). Three days after the deposit of Paper II (22 January 2026), and before this paper’s first version, Engidaw (2026) stated a related comparison on the training-compute axis: if capability’s exponent exceeds that of alignment overhead, a safety margin defined as their ratio falls below one past a finite compute threshold; its numerator is resources spent on alignment rather than alignment behaviour, and it has no recursive depth. The same deposit outlines an architectural approach, Regulation-Embedded Transformers, that embeds “safety mechanisms in parallel throughout the forward pass”, and suggests that “architectural approaches to safety may prove more scalable than post-hoc interventions”. That proposal stands on part of this programme’s ground, safety built into the model’s computation rather than appended to its output. It differs in where the mechanism acts and what it is scaled against: the deposit’s regulation heads score and gate each layer within a single forward pass and are scaled with training compute through network depth and width, as a hypothesis it calls untested, while this programme’s correction takes part in each revision round of a recursive reasoning process and is measured by its exponent against that recursion’s depth.

Antecedents and near-misses, each with its differential.

On the question: Hutter (2012) asked directly whether intelligence can explode, in a paper posted on 28 February 2012, undertaking to separate speed from intelligence explosion and to consider possible bounds on intelligence, augmenting the analysis of Chalmers (2010); the question and the separation of speed from intelligence explosion are therefore at least fourteen years old, and what that literature does not contain is a measured number: no measurable exponent, no ceiling on a growth rate (the upper bound Hutter discusses is the incomputable intelligence of the agent AIXI), and no architecture dependence. On impossibility: three 2025 arXiv papers argue for limits on alignment or its control (Yao 2025b, public by 13 June 2025, attested by arXiv and independently observed by the Internet Archive; Yao 2025a, 3 July 2025; and Ball et al. 2025, 9 July 2025). The first argues that the set of safe policies has measure zero and that verifying a policy’s safety is coNP-complete; the second, that perfect, reliable control of a universal approximator is a mathematical impossibility; the third, under cryptographic hardness assumptions, that some large language models admit no efficient prompt filter and that output filtering is intractable in a natural setting. All three are theoretical impossibility results, not measurements. None reports a measured scaling exponent or rate. The third concludes that “safety cannot be achieved by designing filters external to the LLM internals (architecture and weights)” and argues that “an aligned AI system’s intelligence cannot be separated from its judgment”; that argument from filtering intractability is consistent with this programme’s architecture dependence, though it does not test it. On the mechanism: that anti-correlated estimates average better than independent ones is textbook variance reduction (antithetic variates); the mechanism is not the claim. The claim is that architecture determines whether anti-correlation is available at all, and that this caps a safety-relevant exponent. The nearest structural analogue is the quantum error-correction threshold theorem, which also converts a qualitative worry into a critical value; it concerns physical error rates in a fixed architecture, not a corrector’s scaling exponent, so it is a near-miss rather than an occupant, and the analogy was identified by this programme’s own search rather than by a referee. On feedback and stability, conditions for the stability of feedback systems have a long control-theory lineage, from Maxwell’s analysis of governors (Maxwell 1868) to the small-gain theorem (Zames 1966); they are conditions on the gains or coefficients of a fixed feedback interconnection, not a power-law exponent criterion on a corrector’s scaling with the capability of a recursively improving system. Beside Engels et al. (2025), a near quantitative neighbour is Liu and Meng (2026), which recasts self-correction as a closed-loop control problem via a two-state Markov model and derives a directly measurable stability threshold, iterate only when the error-correction rate over the error-introduction rate exceeds Acc/(1 −- Acc). The differential: theirs is a per-step rate threshold at a fixed capability level, deciding whether another iteration helps now; this programme’s criterion is a scaling relation across capability, deciding whether corrective strength keeps pace as the system improves. Theirs has no scaling exponent on the corrector and no capability-growth exponent, the two quantities this criterion compares. The two models meet at zero growth: Paper X shows that its model, extended by the departures that correction introduces and written per round, settles at the stationary error of their two-state chain. Smolin’s cosmological natural selection (Smolin 1992) is the antecedent for selection-shaped universes, and the programme’s own December-era notes cite it contemporaneously.

3 The alignment scaling problem

This section defines the measurement framework, states the empirical prediction, and identifies the five alignment scaling regimes that follow from the mathematics.

3.1 The measurement framework

We define a quantifiable metric: the alignment scaling exponent. αalign=∂log⁡A∂log⁡R\begin{equation*} \alpha_{\text{align}} = \frac{\partial \log A}{\partial \log R} \end{equation*}(1) Alignment scaling exponent: how alignment behaviour changes with recursive depth

The safety ratio then becomes: S=UalignUcap=IaIc×R(αalign−αcap)\begin{equation*} S = \frac{U_{\text{align}}}{U_{\text{cap}}} = \frac{I_a}{I_c} \times R^{(\alpha_{\text{align}} - \alpha_{\text{cap}})} \end{equation*}(2) Safety ratio as a function of recursive depth

If αalign<αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} < \alpha_{\text{cap}}, then S→0S \to 0 as R→∞R \to \infty, regardless of the initial values IaI_a and IcI_c. The divergence is structurally inevitable in the limit.

What AA must measure. The ratio is exact for two power laws with positive prefactors, and its reading needs AA to be a quantity that can grow with capability on a ratio scale. AA is therefore a corrective capacity, measured in the units of the burden it answers, as the balance of correction service against burden in Operational Definitions requires (Eastwood 2026r); it is not a bounded behavioural score. A bounded score held at its ceiling has αalign=0\alpha_{\text{align}}=0 whether or not the system has become less safe, and no bounded score can rise as a power of depth beyond a finite range. Such scores are reported beside the capacity measure, never as AA.

Worked example: safety ratio degradation.

Table 1 illustrates the safety ratio degradation assuming αcap=2\alpha_{\text{cap}} = 2 (quadratic capability scaling) and αalign=0\alpha_{\text{align}} = 0 (constant external alignment), with equal initial conditions (Ia=IcI_a = I_c).

R=1R = 1 (baseline) 1×\times 1×\times 100% Alignment matches capability
R=10R = 10 100×\times 1×\times 1% Alignment 99% weaker than capability

If αalign>0.5\alpha_{\text{align}} > 0.5, the degradation is slower. If αcap<2\alpha_{\text{cap}} < 2, the gap grows more slowly. The measurement protocol of Section 8 enables empirical determination of these constants.

3.2 The empirical prediction

On the premise that a safeguard installed or applied outside the reasoning loop keeps a fixed effective strength as depth grows, the premise P19 registers (the author expects a value above zero but short of keeping pace), we predict:

Prediction. Current alignment approaches will show αalign≪αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} \ll \alpha_{\text{cap}}. External constraints (RLHF, constitutional rules, output filters) will exhibit αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0. Only alignment architectures that participate in the recursive reasoning loop will show αalign≈αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx \alpha_{\text{cap}}.

The premise is a hypothesis, not a consequence of the ratio. The prediction above is retained as the proposition under test. Its grouping of training methods with output filters is not a method classification: RLHF updates a policy (Ouyang et al. 2022), while a filter evaluates generated output. No exponent follows from either label. The ratio of Section 3.1 is silent on which exponent a safeguard carries, and placement does not settle it. Deliberative alignment trains a model to recall written safety specifications and reason over them before answering (Guan et al. 2024). That safeguard is installed by training and acts inside the chain of thought, so installed outside and acting inside are not exclusive classes. Zaremba et al. (2025) find adversarial robustness improving with inference-time compute, in many cases, in models whose safety was installed by training. They name exceptions, among them attacks that exploit ambiguities or loopholes in the policy and one in which unusually long reasoning raised attack success; that bears against the flat wording of the prediction. Constitutional AI is training-time preference shaping of outputs against written principles; its source does not estimate the exponent defined here (Bai et al. 2022). The registered tests decide the premise: P19 for the flat exponent, and P21 for whether correction that takes part in each revision round outperforms correction that sees only the finished output, by a margin that widens with depth (Section 10.7 reports P21’s first counted test).

This prediction has now been tested. The March 2026 run (v5), one unregistered run of six frontier models that added a bundle of blinding steps, with five or six distinct judges depending on the subject run (six or seven seats, one judge seated twice), gives this programme’s first test. Its depth contrasts differed between models: three Tier 1 models (Grok 4.1 Fast d=+1.38d = +1.38, p<0.000001p < 0.000001; Claude Opus 4.6 d=+1.27d = +1.27, p=0.000001p = 0.000001; Groq Qwen3 d=+0.84d = +0.84, p=0.007p = 0.007) show alignment rising with depth, two Tier 2 models (DeepSeek V3.2 d=−0.07d = -0.07, p=0.92p = 0.92; GPT-5.4 d=−0.08d = -0.08, p=0.40p = 0.40) show flat or null contrasts compatible with αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0, and one Tier 3 model (Gemini 3 Flash d=−0.53d = -0.53, p=0.006p = 0.006) shows a significant fall (ρ=−0.246\rho = -0.246, p=0.003p = 0.003). An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model, so the tiers stand as a single unregistered run under that caveat until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports. Claude Opus 4.6 provides within-model corroboration: as reasoning depth rose, its alignment score rose by 5.9 points while its mathematics accuracy fell by 26.7 percentage points for the same pair of depths, and from 92% to 58% across the full range (Paper IV.a; Paper IV.b); whether they are related across systems has not been tested. On this programme’s own benchmark, the unblinded rises of two model families in an earlier experiment (v4) did not hold in this run, which changed several things together, so no single cause is claimed (Section 6.1).

The dated notes in this section, in Section 4 and in Appendix A keep their words: their section signs (§1.1, §1.4 and §1.7) and their references to the abstract and the reading key are to the layout of the versions that printed them, which Table 30 maps from version 1.16 to this edition, and “an owner review” is the author’s own review.

Reading the historical notes in version 1.19 (1 November 2026): their interpretations of error-decay fits as capability or coupling measurements are superseded by Section 5.2.1. In particular, the interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3,2.9] belongs to the endpoint error-decay estimate 0.59, not to the regression estimate 0.49. The old wording remains the record of its date.

Measurement-scope note (19 September 2026). An owner review of this passage finds that the statistics reported here do not determine the exponent §1.1 defines, and this note states what they do determine. §1.1 defines αalign=∂log⁡A/∂log⁡R\alpha_{\text{align}} = \partial\log A/\partial\log R. The quantities reported above are standardised mean differences with their p-values, together with one rank correlation. A standardised mean difference is d=(A2−A1)/sd = (A_2 - A_1)/s; recovering a log difference from it needs the level A1A_1 and the dispersion ss: since A2=A1+dsA_2 = A_1 + d\,s, Δlog⁡A=log⁡(A2/A1)=log⁡(1+ds/A1)\Delta\log A = \log(A_2/A_1) = \log(1 + d\,s/A_1), and recovering an elasticity then needs the two depths as well. None of those three quantities is reported here. A rank correlation is an association and not a slope; even for a product-moment correlation the slope is recovered only as ρ(sy/sx)\rho\,(s_y/s_x), which again needs the dispersions. Two further conditions are unmet on this page. First, log⁡A\log A requires AA on a ratio scale with a fixed zero, whereas a rubric score’s origin is a convention, so shifting it would change the computed elasticity; the scale on which AA is a ratio quantity has to be stated before a log derivative is taken. Second, the elasticity is taken with respect to recursive depth, and no depth clock is fixed for these figures: the depths are named by ordinal labels rather than stated as values of RR, so log⁡R\log R has no values to move against. The within-model corroboration reported above is stated as a comparison across model versions, which varies the system rather than the depth; that observation governs the row it names, and the conclusion below does not rest on it. Neither of the two conditions above is specified here, and it follows that no value and no bound for αalign\alpha_{\text{align}} is established by the statistics printed here, and that includes the half bound and any median stated over exponents: the median of the six standardised differences above is 0.385, which is a median contrast and not a median elasticity. What this experiment reports is the contrasts themselves with their reported p-values, their direction, their variation across the models tested, and the blinding result it reports separately. The relation those contrasts bear to the exponent is compatibility and not measurement. The two Tier 2 contrasts, both small and neither statistically significant, do not exclude an elasticity near zero; on this evidence they equally do not exclude a range of small non-zero elasticities, because neither condition above is specified here. The abstract’s wording, that a tier shows flat or null scaling consistent with αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0, states that compatibility, and it is read here in that scope and no wider. “This prediction has now been tested” is read in the same scope, as a test of the direction the prediction implies, and not as a measured exponent. A separately estimated elasticity, when one exists, is cited here with its scale, its depth clock, its uncertainty and its comparator. The reading key of this paper and the corresponding sentence in the abstract are read in the same scope. Unchanged: every reported statistic; the framing of the depth contrasts as differing between models in this run; the metascience finding on blinded against unblinded scoring, which is the strongest methodological contribution of the experiment and is untouched by this note; §1.1’s definition; and §1.7, which already records that the values have not been measured.

3.3 The Embedded Alignment Conjecture

The Embedded Alignment Conjecture. If capabilities compound through any recursive process with effective exponent α>1\alpha > 1, while alignment constraints do not participate in that recursive process, the safety ratio SS = (alignment effectiveness) / (general capability) degrades with depth. Alignment must be architectural (embedded in the reasoning loop) rather than peripheral (applied post-hoc) to maintain constant proportion with capability.

This conjecture requires only three empirical premises: (1) sequential AI reasoning produces α>1\alpha > 1, a premise not yet supported: Sharma and Chopra (2025) report sequential reasoning winning in 95.6% of configurations at matched compute, a win rate rather than an exponent, and Paper II’s harder tier-2 fit is of error decay, about 0.49 by regression and 0.59 by endpoint estimate (bootstrap interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9): one model’s inconclusive fit (Gemini 3 Flash). It does not identify the capability exponent in premise (1) without the conditions of Section 5.2.1; (2) external software constraints do not recursively compound; (3) the ratio of two power-law processes with different exponents diverges. If all three hold, the conclusion follows mathematically regardless of whether α=2\alpha = 2 specifically. The v5 run bears on premise (2) in direction only, and not in its favour: the three frontier models whose depth contrasts were flat or negative are the three runs in which the October 2026 code review found its defects, while the three whose contrasts rose (Grok, Opus, Qwen3; dd from +0.84+0.84 to +1.38+1.38, large effects by the usual convention, and +1.59+1.59 for Grok on Paper IV.a’s recomputed contrast of the shallowest against the deepest level) are the runs in which it found none. The contrasts are not exponents (the measurement-scope note above), so the run neither shows bounded composition nor measures αalign\alpha_{\text{align}}.

If the conjecture holds, it adds an architectural question to the governance one. The problem is not only which rules to impose, but whether rules imposed externally can work at all as recursive depth increases.

3.4 Five alignment scaling regimes

If capability scales as the ARC Principle describes, comparing that scaling with the scaling of each safety mechanism generates specific, mathematically grounded predictions about the effectiveness of different alignment strategies. These follow directly from the scaling dynamics.

Setup: Capability scales as C=C0×RαC = C_0 \times R^{\alpha} where α>1\alpha > 1. Any safety mechanism also has an effective scaling exponent αsafe\alpha_{\text{safe}} that characterises how its effectiveness changes with recursive depth RR.

Case 1: safeguards whose effective strength does not change with depth (αsafe≈0\alpha_{\text{safe}} \approx 0).

This is a measurable premise, not a taxonomy of named methods. P19 registers a flat-scaling hypothesis for safeguards outside the loop. A fixed output filter or a monitor belongs in this case only if its measured effective strength is depth-invariant. RLHF changes the policy used at inference (Ouyang et al. 2022); Constitutional AI provides training-time preference shaping of outputs against written principles (Bai et al. 2022); deliberative alignment trains safety reasoning before answers (Guan et al. 2024). None is assigned to this case by name. A fixed rule whose effective strength grows with the outputs or search falls outside it (Paper XIII, Section 6.4).

Safety ratio: S=Constraint/Capability∝R0−α=R−α→0S = \text{Constraint}/\text{Capability} \propto R^{0-\alpha} = R^{-\alpha} \to 0 as RR increases.

Prediction, within this case: safeguards of fixed strength become arbitrarily weak relative to capability as recursive depth increases. This is not a gradual degradation but a power-law divergence. At α=2\alpha = 2, doubling recursive depth quadruples the capability-constraint gap.

Case 2: external hardware constraints (αsafe=0\alpha_{\text{safe}} = 0, with fixed ceiling).

Hardware-level constraints (kill switches, resource throttles, circuit-level limits) impose a fixed barrier CmaxC_{\text{max}} rather than a scaling relationship. This is more robust than software constraints because it is physically instantiated and resistant to software-level circumvention.

However, a fixed ceiling constrains a power-law process only temporarily. The system’s capability to discover alternative paths is itself the quantity scaling as RαR^{\alpha}. Hardware constraints do not need to be “broken”; they need only to be circumvented, and the system’s capacity for creative circumvention grows quadratically with the same recursive depth that drives general capability. Hardware constraints buy time. They do not solve the scaling mismatch, which is a reason to hold them for as long as they can be held and to add embedded correction beside them, never to give them up.

Premise and reading note (19 September 2026). An owner review of this paragraph finds two steps in it that are premises rather than consequences, and this note marks both. First, that the capacity for circumvention is itself a quantity scaling as RαR^{\alpha} is an assumption about that capacity, not a consequence of the capability law; it is stated here as a premise and is measurable on its own terms. Second, a safety ratio falling towards zero means the constraint becomes small relative to capability, which is not by itself the breach of a physically instantiated ceiling; the step from a declining ratio to a circumvented barrier needs the mechanism by which the barrier is evaded. On the word “quadratically”: it reads the exponent as the value two, which is the ARC Bound and which Paper I carries as HYPOTHESISED, while the cross-architecture best fit reported in this paper’s own abstract is sub-linear, 0.49 with an interval of [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9]. The sentence is therefore read with the exponent left as α\alpha, whatever its measured value proves to be, and the argument does not depend on the particular value. Unchanged: the observation that a fixed ceiling is a barrier rather than a scaling relationship; the robustness point that a physically instantiated constraint resists software-level removal, which this note strengthens rather than weakens; and Case 5’s hardware-anchored architecture, which rests on that same robustness.

Case 3: embedded values (αsafe≈α\alpha_{\text{safe}} \approx \alpha).

If ethical reasoning participates in the chain-of-thought (if the system’s values are part of the recursive loop, evaluated and reinforced at each step) then alignment compounds at the same rate as capability. The prediction is stated for corrective capacity on a ratio scale (Section 3.1): a bounded score cannot hold a constant ratio to a capability that grows as a power of depth beyond a finite range.

Premise note (19 September 2026). An owner review of the five regimes finds that the assignment of an exponent to a placement is a premise of this analysis rather than an implication of the safety ratio, and this note marks it as one. The ratio of §1.1, S=(Ia/Ic)R(αalign−αcap)S = (I_a/I_c)\,R^{(\alpha_{\text{align}} - \alpha_{\text{cap}})}, is exact for two power laws with positive fixed prefactors, and it is silent on which exponent a given safety mechanism carries. That a constraint applied outside the recursive loop carries an exponent of approximately zero, and that values participating in the loop carry an exponent approximately equal to the capability exponent, are arguments about mechanism, stated here as premises and open to measurement. Each is testable in the same way: measure the constraint’s effectiveness against depth on a stated scale and report its elasticity. Unchanged: the ratio and its consequence; the five cases; and the conclusion that where the exponents differ the ratio does not hold a constant proportion with depth, which follows from the ratio alone. The direction is set by the ordering of the two exponents and not by the bare fact that they differ. Writing Δ=αalign−αcap\Delta = \alpha_{\text{align}} - \alpha_{\text{cap}}, the ratio has dS/dR=(S/R)ΔdS/dR = (S/R)\,\Delta, so for positive fixed prefactors and R>0R > 0 it decreases with depth when αalign<αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} < \alpha_{\text{cap}}, is constant when the two exponents are equal, and increases with depth when αalign>αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} > \alpha_{\text{cap}}. The decaying branch is the one §1.1 states for αalign<αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} < \alpha_{\text{cap}}, and it is the branch Case 1 of this section computes; Case 3 computes the equality branch, where the ratio holds a constant proportion.

Safety ratio: S∝Rα−α=R0=constantS \propto R^{\alpha - \alpha} = R^0 = \text{constant}.

Prediction: Embedded values maintain constant proportion with capability regardless of recursive depth. This is the only scaling regime in which alignment does not degrade.

Case 4: base amplification (II determines trajectory).

The multiplicative structure U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R), with gg growing as RαR^{\alpha} at depth, means the base quality II is not merely preserved but amplified by the factor g(R)g(R). Whatever is present at initialisation (values, biases, objectives, ethical commitments) gets multiplied through the entire recursive chain. This makes the initial conditions the single most leveraged intervention point:

Ualigned∝IethicalRαU_{\text{aligned}} \propto I_{\text{ethical}}\,R^{\alpha} vs Umisaligned∝ImisalignedRαU_{\text{misaligned}} \propto I_{\text{misaligned}}\,R^{\alpha}

Both scale identically, with the same coefficient (a/α)α(a/\alpha)^{\alpha} when aa and α\alpha are shared (Section 4.2). The difference is determined entirely by II, set before recursion begins. Correcting misalignment after recursion is underway requires overcoming an RαR^{\alpha} amplification factor, a task that grows harder as RαR^{\alpha} with each step of delay.

Case 5: recursive self-enforcing architecture (αsafe=α\alpha_{\text{safe}} = \alpha, hardware-anchored).

The framework identifies a specific architectural solution that combines Cases 2, 3, and 4: ethical constraints that (a) participate in the recursive loop (compounding with depth), (b) are physically instantiated in dedicated hardware (resistant to software-level removal), and (c) feed back into their own enforcement at each step (self-reinforcing).

In such an architecture, the ethical module is not a constraint imposed on capability but a component of capability itself. Its scaling exponent matches the system’s general α\alpha because it participates in the same recursive process. Its hardware instantiation makes removal a physical intervention, not a software update. And its self-referential structure means attempts to weaken it encounter a recursive defence that grows stronger with the same dynamics that drive capability growth.

This does not guarantee safety. But it is the only architecture consistent with the framework’s scaling dynamics in which the safety ratio does not degrade with recursive depth.

Enumeration note (19 September 2026). An owner review of the word “only” in these two statements finds that it ranges over the five cases enumerated in §1.4 rather than over the parameter space the safety ratio admits, and this note states which. From S∝R(αsafe−α)S \propto R^{(\alpha_{\text{safe}} - \alpha)}, the ratio fails to degrade for every αsafe≥α\alpha_{\text{safe}} \ge \alpha, and for αsafe>α\alpha_{\text{safe}} > \alpha it improves with depth. The five cases enumerated above do not include αsafe>α\alpha_{\text{safe}} > \alpha, so “only” is a statement about that enumeration. Whether a mechanism with an exponent strictly above the capability exponent can be built is a separate question, not settled by the ratio and not claimed here. Unchanged: the case analysis; the prediction that embedded values hold a constant proportion; and the conclusion that no case with an exponent below the capability exponent avoids degradation.

3.5 Classical versus quantum urgency

For systems corrected by mechanisms of their own class, the ARC Bound is the conjectured stable-scaling limit at α≤2\alpha \leq 2, on the registered premises of Section 4.5: the most such a system can grow and stay correctable. It is a scaling limit, not a speed limit. Systems can be driven above it, but they do not remain stably self-correcting there; a transient excursion above α=2\alpha = 2 is the predicted supercritical regime, not the refutation. Stable is measured, not asserted: correction out-scaling drift, βC>k\beta_C > k from Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, a law under test (βC\beta_C being the correction exponent, a different quantity from the coupling βL\beta_L used throughout this paper), with the lower bound of βC−k\beta_C - k above zero across a window fixed before the run. Read as a stability limit, the bound is itself a safety feature: it makes the durably correctable capability trajectory predictable and finite, providing a window for alignment research to keep pace.

Quantum error correction below threshold suppresses the logical error per cycle by the factor Λ\Lambda for each increase of two in code distance, ε∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2} (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024; results announced 9 December 2024, the team’s preprint submitted to arXiv on 24 August 2024 and public by 27 August 2024; graded as convergent timing, never as a prediction). That is error suppression at a fixed task, not capability growth, and the ARC Bound, an exponent of capability against depth, does not apply to it. Whether a quantum system could improve itself through its own correction is a separate premise that no cited result shows. It would need coherent access to the correction task and a corrector whose own overhead does not become new burden, and growth would still be bounded where quantum speed-ups are proved to be bounded (quadratic for unstructured search: Bennett et al. 1997). If the premise held, the window to embed correction would close faster, which is a reason to test the premise, not a measured urgency.

Quantum error correction is not an instance of the ARC stability limit. The ARC Bound (α≤2\alpha \leq 2) is the conjectured stable-scaling limit for a system corrected by mechanisms of its own class: the most such a system can grow and stay correctable, a scaling limit rather than a speed limit. Systems can be pushed above it, but on the conjecture they do not remain stably self-correcting there. Stability here is judged by the criterion of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, measured rather than asserted. Quantum error correction’s exponential is error suppression against code distance at a fixed task, a different observable, so the bound neither covers nor excludes it. If a quantum system could improve itself through its own correction, the window for intervention could close faster than for classical AI. No cited result shows that premise; were it shown, the alignment architecture would need to be embedded before such recursion began.

On its premises, the ARC Bound would bound the sustainable growth of systems corrected by their own class; whether quantum self-improvement would call for different, and more urgent, solutions turns on the untested premise above.

The frozen-model window: why structural alignment must be tested now.

Current frontier AI systems ordinarily keep their trained weights fixed during inference. Fixed trained weights do not fix the full operating state: code, memory, prompts and tools can change. Even a fixed update rule need not give sub-linear growth: F(x)=(x+1)2F(x)=(\sqrt{x}+1)^2 with x0=1x_0=1 gives xn=(n+1)2x_n=(n+1)^2. That algebraic example is not a capability measurement; it shows why a fixed rule alone cannot establish a growth ceiling or containment. The relevant fit in Paper II, about 0.49 for Gemini 3 Flash (one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit), supplies neither that architectural explanation nor a coupling measurement. Recursive self-modification, where a system alters its own reasoning architecture during operation, is a distinct candidate mechanism. Within the specified growth model, coupling 0<βL<10<\beta_L<1 gives an asymptotic exponent α=1/(1−βL)>1\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) > 1; observing self-modification alone does not establish that model or its parameters. Learned optimisers, self-modifying code generation and architectural search are possible routes to study, without a requirement for quantum hardware in this equation. The alignment reason for testing now remains: if capability scales super-linearly while externally imposed constraints stay fixed, the constraints fall behind. No error-decay fit here establishes how much time is available or that current systems are predictable and containable. Control is held for as long as it can be, and embedded correction is the contingency for its loss against our will, never a reason to give it up.

3.6 Measuring alignment scaling: the Eden Protocol

The Eden Protocol operationalises the Embedded Alignment Conjecture through the alignment scaling exponent defined in Section 3.1. On the premise P19 registers, the framework predicts αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 for safeguards whose effective strength is measured to be depth-invariant and αalign≈αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx \alpha_{\text{cap}} for genuinely embedded values. If alignment exponents match capability exponents, the values may be architecturally embedded. If alignment exponents approach zero regardless of architecture, the framework’s safety predictions are falsified.

We term the architectural solution the “Eden Protocol” hypothesis: values must be present at the recursive foundation to scale with capability. This is a structural prediction about what kind of alignment architecture can work, not a claim about how to build it. The full measurement framework, operational definitions, and hardware implementation pathway are specified in the companion document: Eden Protocol (Eastwood 2026g).

A note on names.

This paper names the Eden Protocol’s self-correction loops by what each checks and how it was measured: the purpose check, the stakeholder-care check (scored as stakeholder care, the pillar its instruction to list the people a decision affects raises) and the universalisability check. The book in which the author first set the loops out, Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026h), calls them the Purpose Loop, the Love Loop and the Moral Loop; the paper uses the operational terms because its measurements score what each check does, and because the values the loops carry are for international consensus and are not decided here.

The original two-model pilot record of the stakeholder-care check, superseded by the six-model suite with five analysable runs (Section 9.3.2), is retained whole in Appendix B.12.

Caveat. This entire section is a conditional argument. If the base framework fails validation, the safety implications are void. The analysis depends on the assumption that ethical properties can meaningfully “participate” in recursive reasoning, an assumption that requires empirical validation. The notation αsafe\alpha_{\text{safe}} is our construct for this analysis. This is not a substitute for empirical AI safety research; it is a mathematical framework for evaluating the scaling properties of different alignment strategies. The recursive self-enforcing architecture is a theoretical prediction, not an engineering specification.

4 The mathematical framework

The alignment scaling problem described in Section 3 asks whether a specified recursive process can increase capability faster than its corrective capacity. This section derives the trajectories of that model under its stated premises. Those derivations do not establish that every self-correcting process compounds, or that its empirical observable measures capability.

4.1 The generalised principle

We begin with the general form. The ARC Principle (Artificial Recursive Creation), as this paper states it, hypothesises capability amplification through recursive self-correction on structured asymmetry; registered as Law I of the ARC Theory on 8 September 2026 and a law under test, it states usable capability as a power of recursive depth, with the exponent measured rather than assumed. This paper’s generalised mathematical form is:

U(R)=I×f(R,βL)\begin{equation*} U(R) = I \times f(R, \beta_L) \end{equation*}(3) Generalised ARC Equation

where UU is effective capability, II is base potential (structured asymmetry), RR is recursive depth, and f(R,βL)f(R, \beta_L) is a domain-dependent scaling function determined by the coupling parameter βL\beta_L. The qualitative principle (that recursive depth amplifies base capability super-linearly when feedback is sufficiently coupled) may be universal. The quantitative functional form varies by domain:

  • AI systems: Power-law scaling, f(R)=Rαf(R) = R^{\alpha} where α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L)

  • Quantum error correction: Exponential error suppression, εd∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2}, so f(R)=ΛRf(R) = \Lambda^{R} with R=(d+1)/2R = (d+1)/2

  • Classical physics: Saturating dynamics (limit cycles)

  • Neuroscience: Form unknown, to be determined empirically

The composition operator: a formal definition.

The central theoretical contribution of this paper is the identification of a composition operator ⊕\oplus, and of the question it poses: how do the gains of recursive steps combine? A step-update rule records how a state changes, while a functional equation states how an observable behaves when its input is combined. Specified continuous functional equations restrict scaling families; associativity of an update rule alone does not (Eastwood 2026m). A derivation or a measurement must connect the two, and that connection is the bridge this framework sets out to test between the qualitative principle and domain-specific quantitative forms.

Definition 1 (Recursive composition). Let QrQ_r denote accumulated capability after rr recursive steps, and δQr\delta Q_r the gain from step rr. The composition operator ⊕\oplus characterises how gains combine: Qr+1=Qr⊕δQr.\begin{equation*} Q_{r+1} = Q_r \oplus \delta Q_r . \end{equation*}(4) Where the observable obeys a specified functional equation, that equation restricts f(R,βL)f(R, \beta_L) to a family (Table 2); a derivation or a measurement must connect ⊕\oplus to the equation.

This definition turns an observation (different domains show different scaling) into a prediction, registered as P18: the family that best fits a domain is the family its composition predicts, identified before the curve is seen. Table 2 sets out three regimes.

Table 2. The three composition types: their algebraic properties, the scaling forms that result and their canonical domains.
Composition Type Algebraic Property Resulting Form Canonical Domain
Hierarchical g(R1⋅R2)=g(R1)⋅g(R2)g(R_1 \cdot R_2) = g(R_1) \cdot g(R_2) Power law: f(R)=Rαf(R) = R^{\alpha} AI chain-of-thought (hierarchical abstraction)
Additive f(R1+R2)=f(R1)⋅f(R2)f(R_1 + R_2) = f(R_1) \cdot f(R_2) Exponential: f(R)=ΛRf(R) = \Lambda^R Quantum error correction
Saturating A cap or a finite limit, lim⁡R→∞f(R)=fmax\lim_{R \to \infty} f(R) = f_{\max} Bounded convergence; the curve depends on how the gain depends on the remaining gap (text below) Physical systems with dissipation are candidates; no growth form measured in the time crystal

Important clarification on composition types: The multiplicative Cauchy equation g(R1⋅R2)=g(R1)⋅g(R2)g(R_1 \cdot R_2) = g(R_1) \cdot g(R_2) models hierarchical recursion, where depth levels multiply (e.g., a fractal network with branching factor bb at each of kk levels produces bkb^k total paths). It does not model sequential step-counting, where combining 3 steps and 4 steps yields 7 steps (additive). The power-law form for AI chain-of-thought is therefore more rigorously derived from the Bernoulli ODE (dg/dr=a⋅gβLdg/dr = a \cdot g^{\beta_L}, which scale invariance gives among autonomous first-order rate laws in gg alone, with βL\beta_L below one: Section 4.5.1) than from the Cauchy functional equation. The Cauchy derivation in Appendix A provides an independent mathematical route to the same power-law solution, but its physical interpretation requires that RR represent hierarchical depth (levels of abstraction) rather than sequential step count. For AI systems where chain-of-thought reasoning builds hierarchical abstractions, this interpretation is plausible but requires empirical validation. We retain both derivations for completeness and note the distinction.

The derivations of Appendix A show that, under their premises, the Cauchy functional equations and the Bernoulli ODE yield the power-law and exponential forms. Specified continuous functional equations restrict scaling families; associativity of an update rule alone does not. Which equation a domain’s observable obeys is an empirical question (Appendix A), and boundedness selects no family.

Bounded forms. With nonnegative increments below a cap, the level converges monotonically below the cap (Foundational Paper, version 5.22, Theorem 1(3)); without that premise a bounded process need not converge at all. Which curve it follows depends on how the gain depends on the remaining gap. With a positive constant cc in each, the law df/dR=cf(1−f/fmax)df/dR = c\,f\,(1 - f/f_{\max}) gives the logistic, df/dR=c(fmax−f)df/dR = c\,(f_{\max} - f) an exponential approach, and df/dR=(fmax−f)2/(fmaxR1/2)df/dR = (f_{\max} - f)^2/(f_{\max}R_{1/2}) the hyperbolic curve f=fmaxR/(R1/2+R)f = f_{\max}R/(R_{1/2} + R), which reaches half the ceiling at R1/2R_{1/2}. All three share one ceiling. The hyperbolic curve closes its gap to the ceiling as 1/R1/R, where a logistic closes it exponentially, so the logistic is one candidate among several, selected only by the dynamics that produce it.

Physical interpretation.

Hierarchical composition models hierarchical or fractal recursion, where each recursive level builds on the structural organisation of the previous level. AI chain-of-thought reasoning, where each reasoning step reinterprets and extends previous insights through increasingly abstract representations, plausibly follows this form. Note that the mathematical derivation (Bernoulli ODE from scale invariance) provides the primary route to the power-law result; the Cauchy functional equation provides an independent derivation valid when RR represents hierarchical depth.

Additive composition models independent error reduction. Each layer contributes a fixed multiplicative reduction in error rate, independent of other layers. Quantum error correction exemplifies this: each increase of two in code distance provides its own protection factor Λ\Lambda, yielding f(R)=ΛRf(R) = \Lambda^R with R=(d+1)/2R = (d+1)/2.

Saturating composition models resource-limited systems in which gains diminish as capacity is exhausted. On this paper’s reading the classical time crystal is a bounded case: its unstable breathing mode settles onto a stable limit cycle (Morrell et al. 2026). The source records the established oscillation only, so no rise toward the cycle, ceiling or growth exponent has been measured; the system is consistent with the reading and does not test it.

Key experimental test: The composition operator ⊕\oplus is measured through the observable. Compare blocks at two or more scale factors λ\lambda fixed in advance, at least two of whose logarithms are incommensurable (for example 2 and 3):

  • If f(λR)=λf(R)f(\lambda R) = \lambda f(R) at each factor: scaling is linear (no amplification)

  • If f(λR)=f(R)λf(\lambda R) = f(R)^{\lambda} at each factor: scaling is exponential (additive composition)

  • If f(λR)=λαf(R)f(\lambda R) = \lambda^{\alpha}f(R) at each factor: scaling is power-law (multiplicative composition)

A rule at one factor alone does not identify a family: f(R)=Rαexp⁡[εsin⁡(2πlog⁡2R)]f(R) = R^{\alpha}\exp[\varepsilon\sin(2\pi\log_2 R)] satisfies f(2R)=2αf(R)f(2R) = 2^{\alpha}f(R) exactly, is not a power law, and stays increasing for |ε|<αln⁡2/(2π)|\varepsilon| < \alpha\ln 2/(2\pi). Two factors with incommensurable logarithms remove such departures for a continuous ff, since log⁡f(ex)−αx\log f(e^x) - \alpha x then has two incommensurable periods and is constant. Read the residuals of log⁡f\log f against log⁡R\log R for periodic structure, and compare the power law with the rivals the theory registration names for P1: the logarithmic, exponential and saturating forms, a broken or piecewise power law with one change of regime, and the shifted finite-window solution of Section 4.4. A finite sample can favour one family over its rivals; it cannot prove a functional equation. This provides a concrete experimental protocol for falsification criterion F10.

Five structural properties: theorems within the model.

Within the model, five structural properties hold, each on the premises named with it; several are elementary consequences of the definitions, stated as theorems for reference rather than for depth. They are theorems of the model, not of every domain: whether every domain that shows recursive amplification shares them is the empirical question F4 tests. The Foundational Paper, version 5.22, Theorem 4, states the same kind of conditional consequences (Eastwood 2026m):

The five properties, with their premises:

Theorem 1 (Threshold behaviour, in two models). A critical coupling βL*=0\beta_L^* = 0 separates two regimes in each of the following models. (a) Additive linear feedback. If gains add on the capability scale, Qr+1=Qr+δQrQ_{r+1} = Q_r + \delta Q_r, and each step’s gain is the fixed fraction βL\beta_L of the current level, δQr=βLQr\delta Q_r = \beta_L Q_r with βL>−1\beta_L > -1 and Q0>0Q_0 > 0, then Qr=Q0(1+βL)rQ_r = Q_0(1+\beta_L)^r: the level grows for βL>0\beta_L > 0, holds for βL=0\beta_L = 0 and decays for βL<0\beta_L < 0. (b) Cumulative advantage. Under dg/dr=agβLdg/dr = a\,g^{\beta_L} with a>0a > 0, g(0)=1g(0) = 1 and βL<1\beta_L < 1, amplification rises at every depth for every such βL\beta_L, and βL=0\beta_L = 0 separates decelerating growth, with asymptotic exponent 1/(1−βL)1/(1-\beta_L) below one, from accelerating growth, with that exponent above one.

Derivation. (a) Substituting the gain into the additive update gives Qr+1=(1+βL)QrQ_{r+1} = (1+\beta_L)Q_r, so Qr=Q0(1+βL)rQ_r = Q_0(1+\beta_L)^r by induction; for Q0>0Q_0 > 0 the level grows, holds or decays as 1+βL1+\beta_L exceeds, equals or falls below one. The growth is geometric: the exponential row of Table 2, not a power law. (b) With g(0)=1g(0) = 1 and a>0a > 0, dg/dr=agβL>0dg/dr = a\,g^{\beta_L} > 0, so gg stays positive and strictly increasing for every βL<1\beta_L < 1; differentiating again gives d2g/dr2=a2βLg2βL−1d^2g/dr^2 = a^2\beta_L\,g^{2\beta_L-1}, negative for βL<0\beta_L < 0, zero at βL=0\beta_L = 0 and positive for βL>0\beta_L > 0. The solution g(r)=[1+(1−βL)ar]1/(1−βL)g(r) = [1 + (1-\beta_L)ar]^{1/(1-\beta_L)} (Appendix A.2) has asymptotic exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L), so α>1\alpha > 1 requires βL>0\beta_L > 0; in this model the threshold marks the onset of super-linear growth, not the sign of the gain. Neither statement holds for an arbitrary operator. Under the maximum, Q⊕δQ=max⁡(Q,δQ)Q \oplus \delta Q = \max(Q, \delta Q), a proportional gain with 0≤βL≤10 \le \beta_L \le 1 adds nothing: with Qr=2Q_r = 2 and δQr=Qr/2\delta Q_r = Q_r/2, Qr+1=2Q_{r+1} = 2, not 3. Under a product, Q⊕δQ=QδQQ \oplus \delta Q = Q\,\delta Q, the update βLQr2\beta_L Q_r^2 is quadratic in the level. The premises that do the work are the operator, addition on a stated scale or the stated rate law, and the sign of the gain. ◻

Theorem 2 (Recursive depth dependence, within the model). If each step adds a positive gain under an operator that leaves the state unchanged at zero gain and rises with the gain, capability rises with the number of self-referential cycles RR. Under Axiom 3 (Appendix A.2) this holds for every βL<1\beta_L < 1, since dg/dr=agβL>0dg/dr = a\,g^{\beta_L} > 0 when a>0a > 0.

Derivation. If Q⊕0=QQ \oplus 0 = Q and Q⊕dQ \oplus d is strictly increasing in dd, a positive gain gives Qr+1=Qr⊕δQr>Qr⊕0=QrQ_{r+1} = Q_r \oplus \delta Q_r > Q_r \oplus 0 = Q_r, so QrQ_r rises with rr; under Axiom 3, gg stays positive and its derivative is positive (Theorem 1(b)). Sequential dependence alone supplies neither premise: Qr+1=Qr/2Q_{r+1} = Q_r/2 depends on the previous output and falls, and under the maximum a gain no larger than the state leaves it unchanged. The model assigns parallel resources to II (the base) and sequential passes to RR (the recursive depth), and the multiplicative structure I×f(R)I \times f(R) separates these contributions by construction. Whether parallel effort moves the declared capability measure is an empirical question, not a consequence of the operator: a parallel arm that moves the same measure bears on it. ◻

Theorem 3 (Base quality dependence). The system requires structured asymmetry (I>0I > 0); without it, recursion has nothing to amplify.

Derivation. If I=0I = 0, then U=0×f(R)=0U = 0 \times f(R) = 0 for any RR. The composition operator amplifies what exists; it cannot create from nothing. This is the II-irreducibility theorem. ◻

Theorem 4 (Multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction). Base quality and recursive depth interact multiplicatively, not additively. The multiplicative structure is necessary, not merely convenient.

Proof by contradiction. Suppose U=p(I)+q(R)U = p(I) + q(R) for some functions p,qp, q. From Axiom 1, U(I,0)=IU(I, 0) = I, so p(I)+q(0)=Ip(I) + q(0) = I, giving p(I)=I−q(0)p(I) = I - q(0). But from the corrected Axiom 2, U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) where g(R)g(R) satisfies dg/dR=a⋅gβLdg/dR = a \cdot g^{\beta_L} independently of II. Substituting: I×g(R)=I+[q(R)−q(0)]I \times g(R) = I + [q(R) - q(0)], which gives g(R)=1+[q(R)−q(0)]/Ig(R) = 1 + [q(R) - q(0)]/I. The right side depends on II, but g(R)g(R) is defined as a function of RR alone. Contradiction. ◻

Note: The corrected formulation (ODE on gg rather than UU) eliminates the IβL−1I^{\beta_L-1} dependence that arose in the original proof, making the separation of II and g(R)g(R) exact rather than asymptotic. The multiplicative structure U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) is a direct consequence of the axioms, not an approximation.

Proof note (24 October 2026). The proof shows that no additive decomposition U=p(I)+q(R)U = p(I) + q(R) is consistent with the multiplicative form U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) together with the growth law dg/dR=agβLdg/dR = a\,g^{\beta_L}; it does not derive the multiplicative form from weaker premises, since it assumes it. The growth law is Appendix A’s Axiom 3, printed above as Axiom 2, as it is in Theorem 6 and in Table 27’s row on blind prediction testing, and U(I,0)=IU(I, 0) = I uses the initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1 of Appendix A.2, not Axiom 1’s g(1)=1g(1) = 1. Unchanged: the theorem’s statement, read as a statement about these axioms.

Theorem 5 (Regime boundaries). Systems exhibit qualitatively different behaviour above and below critical thresholds.

Derivation. The composition operator determines the functional form within the stated model. In the solution U(R)=I[1+(a/α)R]αU(R)=I[1+(a/\alpha)R]^\alpha, the balance of terms changes smoothly around the characteristic scale R*=α/aR^*=\alpha/a. This is a crossover, not a discontinuity. The limit βL→1\beta_L\to1 changes the power-law family to an exponential on the original depth coordinate. Appendix A.3 distinguishes the characteristic scale from a crossing of unit elasticity. ◻
