In the solution of Section 4.4, U(R)=I×[1+(a/α)R]αU(R) = I \times [1 + (a/\alpha)R]^{\alpha}, the change of dominant term is a change of regime in scaling behaviour: a smooth crossover, not a discontinuity or a phase transition. Unchanged: the theorem’s statement.

These five properties constitute the qualitative ARC Principle within the model. Each holds on the premises named with it, so accepting those premises commits one to all five. Whether a domain satisfies the premises, and which functional form its observable takes, are empirical questions: the properties are theorems of the model, not of every domain.

4.2 The AI-specific form: power-law scaling

For AI systems exhibiting multiplicative composition, the generalised equation in the deep recursion regime (R≫R*=α/aR \gg R^* = \alpha/a) reduces to:

U≈I(aα)αRα\begin{equation*} U \approx I \left(\frac{a}{\alpha}\right)^{\alpha} R^{\alpha} \end{equation*}(5) Effective capability in the deep recursion limit: base potential ×\times a coefficient set by the recursion ×\times recursive depthα^{\alpha}

Measured in units of the crossover scale, x=1+R/R*x = 1 + R/R^*, the solution is exactly U=I×xαU = I \times x^{\alpha}, with II the value at zero added depth on either clock. The exact integrated form, derived in Section 4.4, is U(R)=I×[1+aαR]αU(R) = I \times [1 + \frac{a}{\alpha}R]^{\alpha}. The pure power law in RR is its asymptotic limit when recursive depth substantially exceeds the characteristic scale R*R^*, and the coefficient (a/α)α(a/\alpha)^{\alpha} stays: it is built from the recursion’s parameters and is not absorbed into II. Neither R*R^* nor that regime has been identified by the AI error-decay fits reported here. Applying those fits to the capability model requires the metric and coordinate conditions of Section 5.2.1; Appendix A.3 gives the finite-depth elasticity.

In plain language: once recursion runs well past its crossover scale, effective capability (UU) grows as the starting potential (II) times the recursive depth (RR) raised to a power (α\alpha) that depends on how well each step builds on the previous one, scaled by a constant the recursion sets.

4.3 What each variable means

UU: effective capability.

What the system actually achieves. Measured differently in each domain:

  • AI: A declared benchmark measure, such as accuracy; inverse error is a different, explicitly chosen proxy (Section 5.2.1)

  • Quantum: Logical qubit fidelity (how error-free the computation is)

  • Physics: Temporal stability of the time crystal

  • Biology: Metabolic efficiency (thermodynamic) or cognitive task performance (behavioural)

II: base potential (structured asymmetry).

Thermodynamic definition: Natural systems tend towards maximum entropy (equilibrium/uniformity). In this framework, “artificial” denotes any system maintaining low-entropy structure against the thermodynamic gradient, whether engineered (an AI model), evolved (a brain), or emergent (a time crystal). The parameter II measures how far from maximum entropy the system starts.

In Morrell, Elliott and Grier’s analysis, identical beads interact reciprocally and no active region exists: “The active region vanishes for particles of the same size (a1=a2a_1 = a_2), whose interactions are reciprocal” (Morrell et al. 2026). The framework reads this as an instance of its zero-factor property, a correspondence of structure and not a test. Order requires designed disorder: a specific pattern of asymmetry that enables work extraction from the environment.

Table 3. What the base potential II measures in each domain, and its physical meaning.
Domain What II measures Physical meaning
AI Single-pass value of the chosen task metric Baseline on that same metric; accuracy and inverse error are not interchangeable
Quantum Raw qubit quality (1−1 - error rate) Distance from maximum entropy
Physics Variance in bead sizes Asymmetry enabling nonreciprocal forces
Biology Initial learning rate Sensitivity gradient

The Constraint Principle: Constraint enables competence. Without structured asymmetry, no work can be extracted. The time-crystal case above is the physical correspondence; criterion F3 grades it a correspondence of structure, not a test (Table 21).

RR: recursive depth.

How many self-referential cycles the system performs. The output of cycle nn becomes the input for cycle n+1n+1.

Table 4. One unit of recursive depth RR in each domain, and how it is counted.
Domain One unit of RR How it is counted

Quantum One step of two in code distance Code distance dd, with R=(d+1)/2R = (d+1)/2
Physics One oscillation period Frequency analysis
Biology One feedback cycle Generation or learning iteration

Critical requirement: For α>1\alpha > 1, recursion must incorporate sequential self-correction: each step building on previous outputs. Pure parallel processing (independent attempts averaged together) cannot achieve α>1\alpha > 1 because it lacks the output→\toinput feedback loop. However, hybrid parallel-sequential methods have outperformed both parallel-only and sequential-only baselines in code generation (Li et al. 2025); whether they achieve intermediate scaling is untested.

α\alpha: the scaling exponent.

The scaling exponent determines the system’s scaling regime:

α<1\alpha < 1 Diminishing returns Parallel voting: more samples help less and less
α=1\alpha = 1 Linear returns Each step adds a fixed amount
α>1\alpha > 1 Increasing returns Each step adds more than the one before

Our core prediction: αsequential>1>αparallel\alpha_{\text{sequential}} > 1 > \alpha_{\text{parallel}}

4.4 Deriving α\alpha from first principles

Within the cumulative-advantage model, α\alpha is fixed by βL\beta_L: α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L). The identity turns α\alpha into a prediction only when βL\beta_L and aa are measured on records disjoint from the trajectory to be predicted, on the same declared observable and depth clock (Foundational Paper, version 5.22, Section 3.3); without such a measurement it restates a fitted α\alpha as a βL\beta_L.

The key insight.

How much does your accumulated knowledge help your next step?

Define βL∈[0,1)\beta_L \in [0, 1) as the “self-referential coupling”: the log elasticity of marginal gain with respect to accumulated amplification. From the governing equation below, log⁡(dg/dr)=log⁡a+βLlog⁡g\log(dg/dr) = \log a + \beta_L\log g, so βL\beta_L says how strongly the gain of the next step grows with what has accumulated, and the numerical check below estimates it from marginal gains in log-log space. A fraction of accumulated context, or of tokens, is a different quantity and would need its own operational definition before βL\beta_L could be read as one. The domain restriction βL<1\beta_L < 1 is what makes α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) finite and the power-law form exist. At βL=1\beta_L = 1 the solution is the exponential eaRe^{aR}, finite at every finite depth; a finite-depth divergence belongs to βL>1\beta_L > 1, where gg diverges at the depth 1/[a(βL−1)]1/[a(\beta_L-1)]. As βL\beta_L rises towards one the exponent diverges while the solution converges pointwise to the exponential: at a=1a = 1 and R=3R = 3 it is 13.79 at βL=0.9\beta_L = 0.9, 19.22 at βL=0.99\beta_L = 0.99 and 20.00 at βL=0.999\beta_L = 0.999, against e3=20.09e^{3} = 20.09.

At βL=0\beta_L = 0 the marginal gain does not depend on what has accumulated, and growth is linear (α=1\alpha = 1).
As βL\beta_L approaches one, the asymptotic exponent grows without bound.

The mathematics.

Since U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R), the compounding operates on the amplification factor g(R)g(R), not on the absolute capability UU. The marginal amplification gained at step rr depends on accumulated amplification:

dgdr=a×gβL\begin{equation*} \frac{dg}{dr} = a \times g^{\beta_L} \end{equation*}(6)

Why this form? This differential equation models cumulative advantage (also called preferential attachment; Barabási and Albert 1999): the rate of amplification gain is proportional to the system’s current amplification raised to a power. Critically, the ODE operates on gg (the amplification factor) rather than UU (the absolute capability), ensuring that the base intelligence II acts purely as a multiplicative starting constant and does not contaminate the recursive dynamics. This resolves an algebraic inconsistency present in earlier versions of this paper (see Ledger Note 1 in the Version history (Appendix B.11)).

Solving this differential equation (details in Appendix A) with initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1 yields:

U(R)=I×[1+aαR]αwhereα=11−βL\begin{equation*} U(R) = I \times \left[ 1 + \frac{a}{\alpha} R \right]^{\alpha} \quad \text{where} \quad \alpha = \frac{1}{1 - \beta_L} \end{equation*}(7) The corrected ARC equation (exact integrated form)

In the deep recursion limit (R≫α/aR \gg \alpha/a) the bracket tends to (a/α)R(a/\alpha)R, so U≈I(a/α)αRαU \approx I\,(a/\alpha)^{\alpha}R^{\alpha}, the power-law form of equation (5); the empirical sections fit exponents rather than amplitudes, so no reported result depends on the coefficient. The coefficient is not near one in general: it is 0.25 at α=2\alpha = 2 with a=1a = 1, 0.0625 at α=2\alpha = 2 with a=0.5a = 0.5, 0.68 at α=1.33\alpha = 1.33 with a=1a = 1, and 0.037 at α=3\alpha = 3 with a=1a = 1. It may not be absorbed into II: it is built from the recursion parameters, and the rate law acts on the amplification factor precisely so that II stays a multiplicative constant outside the recursive dynamics. Where an amplitude is fitted to data, the fitted amplitude is I(a/α)αI\,(a/\alpha)^{\alpha}, not II.

What this means.

Hypothesis: richer critique-and-revise loops raise the measured coupling βL\beta_L, tested by estimating βL\beta_L before and after such a change, at fixed weights and resources, on one declared observable. Nothing in the model makes βL\beta_L rise with richer self-correction, so this is a hypothesis, not a consequence. The value two is no destination for α\alpha: it is the ARC Bound, the conjectured ceiling for same-class correction on the premises of Section 4.5.

A numerical check of the identity.

The βL\beta_L-derivation is not a curve fit. It is a mathematical identity recoverable to machine precision. To verify this, the relationship α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) was tested against 30 exact solutions to the Bernoulli ODE with βL\beta_L values spanning 0.05 to 0.92. The procedure measures βL\beta_L blindly from marginal gains (dg/dRdg/dR vs gg in log-log space), predicts α\alpha, and compares against the true value. The result: R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000 (eight decimal places), slope =1.000102= 1.000102, mean absolute prediction error =0.002%= 0.002\%. The identity is exact by the derivation above; this numerical check confirms only that the estimation procedure recovers it from the ODE’s own solutions, and is no evidence that a real system obeys the ODE.

4.5 The ARC Bound

The ARC framework makes a central, falsifiable conjecture: a system corrected by mechanisms of its own class does not sustain a scaling exponent above α=2\alpha = 2 while it stays correctable. The value comes from Law III, the ARC Ceiling (a law under test), αcrit=1/(1−χ)\alpha_{\text{crit}} = 1/(1-\chi), where χ\chi is the correction-leverage exponent, written γ\gamma in the registration’s frozen notation: the ceiling returns two at χ=1/2\chi = 1/2 and at most two for χ≤1/2\chi \leq 1/2, the cap that P6 of the theory registration conjectures for same-class correctors. Two is therefore the output of a conditional model at its registered parameter value, not a measured ceiling. Its premises are those version 1.104 of the registration states (Eastwood 2026n). First, the ceiling relation holds. It is a conditional specialisation of the balance between correction and burden in Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law: the burden model fixes the drift exponent, the direct depth term is zero, capability sits on a justified ratio scale and the stated correction model applies. Second, P6 holds for the corrector’s declared class; the registration holds P6 with low confidence and admits no supported verdict on it. Third, the boundary takes the relation’s form (P20). The registration claims the inequality, at most two, and conjectures the equality, which would also need P17 and a mapping it has not registered. In the cumulative-advantage model of Section 4.4, where α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L), the bound α≤1/(1−χ)\alpha \leq 1/(1-\chi) reads βL≤χ\beta_L \leq \chi, the ordering study AG is designed to test; at P6’s cap it is βL≤0.5\beta_L \leq 0.5. Stability is judged by the criterion of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law.

4.5.1 Scale-free derivation

The rate law of the growth model follows from scale invariance together with three further premises, which this subsection names. Consider a system whose capability U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) depends on recursive depth and base quality, and restrict attention to autonomous first-order rate laws dg/dr=F(g)dg/dr = F(g) in which the marginal gain depends on the accumulated amplification alone, with FF positive and continuous. Invariance under the joint rescaling g→λgg \to \lambda g, r→λ1−βLrr \to \lambda^{1-\beta_L}r for every λ>0\lambda > 0 requires F(λg)=λβLF(g)F(\lambda g) = \lambda^{\beta_L}F(g), so F(g)=F(1)gβLF(g) = F(1)\,g^{\beta_L}:

dgdr=a⋅gβL\begin{equation*} \frac{dg}{dr} = a \cdot g^{\beta_L} \end{equation*}(8) Bernoulli ODE operating on amplification factor (scale-invariant form), with a=F(1)a = F(1)

Autonomy, first order and a rate that depends on gg alone are premises, not consequences of the symmetry, and a rate with terms in two different powers, such as a polynomial with fixed coefficients, is invariant under no single joint rescaling. The symmetry does not exclude the exponential: dg/dr=agdg/dr = a\,g is the member βL=1\beta_L = 1, invariant under g→λgg \to \lambda g with rr unchanged. This paper restricts βL\beta_L below one so that α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) is finite, and that restriction, not scale invariance, is what excludes the exponential. The solutions are not themselves scale-free: the initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1 breaks the symmetry and, with the rate aa, fixes the crossover scale R*=α/aR^* = \alpha/a (Theorem 5).

The solution is g(r)=[1+aαr]αg(r) = [1 + \frac{a}{\alpha}r]^{\alpha} where α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L), so it approaches a pure power only for depth well beyond R*R^*: g(r)∝r1/(1−βL)g(r) \propto r^{1/(1-\beta_L)} in the deep recursion limit. The derivation chain is:

  1. Scale invariance, among autonomous first-order rate laws in gg alone, gives the power rate agβLa\,g^{\beta_L}; the restriction βL<1\beta_L < 1 is a further premise

  2. The Bernoulli ODE yields the shifted power solution, a pure power on the crossover clock and asymptotically in RR

  3. The asymptotic exponent is determined by the coupling: α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L)

  4. Law III, the ARC Ceiling, αcrit=1/(1−χ)\alpha_{\text{crit}} = 1/(1-\chi), caps the exponent a system can sustain while correction keeps pace; in this model α≤αcrit\alpha \leq \alpha_{\text{crit}} reads βL≤χ\beta_L \leq \chi

  5. Therefore, where the corrector is of the system’s own class and P6’s conjectured cap χ≤1/2\chi \leq 1/2 holds, α≤2\alpha \leq 2: the ARC Bound, on the premises above

The ARC Bound (a conjecture). For a system corrected by mechanisms of its own class, the bound is α≤2\alpha\leq2 (equivalently βL≤0.5\beta_L\leq0.5 in the stated model, at P6’s cap): the value Law III, the ARC Ceiling, returns at the same-class cap P6 conjectures, on the registered premises above. The transport exponent αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1 belongs to a different model and observable pair, with demand, route-length and measurement assumptions (Section 5.6); finite-dimensional embedding alone does not establish it. Earlier biological and transport accounts are compared under their own assumptions (West et al. 1997, 1999; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010; Demetrius 2003; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013). On the Origin of Scaling Laws, version 3.15 (revised 9 November 2026; first-publication record 22 February 2026), separates this conditional transport route from Cauchy’s classification of form. The quantum error-correction exponential considered here is outside those power-law models. The capability bound has not been independently tested; F11 states the condition that would refute it.

The initial error-decay estimate αerr≈2.2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.2 from the author’s Paper II experiment (N=12N = 12, 95% CI 1.5 to 3.0; the DeepSeek R1 run of 21 January 2026) was followed by a replication across the five frontier models of its capability arm with 30 problems (Paper II, March 2026; Eastwood 2026c). The author retracted the early estimate when that larger study did not reproduce it; the source attributes it to a small sample, a single model and a compressed accuracy range. The old comparison of 2.2 and [1.5, 3.0] with the conjectured capability bound α≤2\alpha\leq2 (criteria F5 and F11) required a metric bridge that was not established. A wide error-fit interval is not a confidence interval for the capability bound. The surviving Gemini 3 Flash error-decay estimates are about 0.49 by regression and 0.59 by endpoint, the latter with bootstrap interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9: one model’s inconclusive fit.

The earlier argument from attention, withdrawn.

Versions up to 1.20 argued the value two from the O(N2)O(N^2) operation count of transformer self-attention. That argument is withdrawn, as the Foundational Paper withdrew it at version 5.22, and the value two and its name stay. The count measures the cost of attention over NN tokens; it bounds neither task capability against recursive depth nor the coupling βL\beta_L. Composed dependence is not quadratic either: in a causal graph in which every position attends to every earlier one, the number of directed paths from the first position to the NN-th is 2N−22^{N-2} (8, 256 and 262,144 at N=5N = 5, 10 and 20). Nor does a cost count fix an exponent: NN independent checks combined by a majority vote cost O(N)O(N), yet the error of the decision falls exponentially in NN. The coupling reading that went with the argument, in which each step uses a fixed share of accumulated context, gives βL\beta_L a meaning it does not have: βL\beta_L is an elasticity (Section 4.4).

Empirical status. The original error-decay estimate αerr≈2.2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.2 (N=12N=12, 95% CI 1.5 to 3.0) is retracted. The later Paper II study (March 2026) covered five frontier models and 30 problems (18 AIME-level), with bootstrap CIs and cross-verification, and did not reproduce it. Its cleanest regression fit is about 0.49, one inconclusive Gemini 3 Flash error-decay estimate (Section 6.2). The old comparison of 2.2 and [1.5, 3.0] with α≤2\alpha\leq2 conflated estimands. The ARC Bound is neither confirmed nor refuted by those fits without the metric and growth-model identification in Section 5.2.1.

Scope of the bound: The registered scope is the same-class corrector: a system corrected by mechanisms of its own class, with the class declared and evidenced before the run. A cross-class system measured above two does not refute the bound. No architectural label alone establishes or escapes it, since the ceiling is conditional on the registered correction and burden model. The wider reach of earlier versions, to every classical sequential system, is this paper’s own early conjecture, criterion F11, and decides nothing registered. The bound does not apply to quantum error correction, whose exponential is error suppression against code distance at a fixed task, a different observable (Section 5.3). Previous versions of this paper offered three arguments for the bound: an elasticity analysis, an edge-of-chaos derivation and the attention count. All three are withdrawn: elasticity exceeding unity does not imply dynamical instability; a one-dimensional autonomous ODE cannot be chaotic, since its trajectories are monotone; and the attention count bounds neither capability against depth nor composed dependence.

The ARC Bound therefore identifies a conjectured stable-scaling limit: the most a system corrected by mechanisms of its own class can grow while remaining correctable, on the registered premises; it is a scaling limit, not a speed limit. Limits of this kind are familiar from thermodynamics: a ceiling on a class of mechanism, which no engineering within the class can exceed. Systems can be driven above it, but on the conjecture they do not remain stably self-correcting there; a transient excursion above the bound is the predicted supercritical regime, not the refutation. Stability here is judged by the criterion of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law (a law under test), measured rather than asserted. Escaping the bound stably needs a corrector outside the class, whose leverage exponent the cap does not bind (Section 2 sets this beside the slope comparison of Engels et al. 2025), just as escaping a mechanism-class ceiling in thermodynamics requires a different mechanism class, not a better instance of the old one.

Scope across domains.

The ceiling discussed here is conditional on the registered correction and burden model, and no architectural label alone establishes or escapes it. The wider reach of earlier versions, to every system governed by multiplicative composition, biological transport networks, economic hierarchies and scale-free graphs among them, is withdrawn. The theory registration places biological and economic systems out of scope, as systems “for which the framework offers an analogy and no measurement”, and biological transport under this paper’s own conditional model has a different observable and an exponent αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C = d/(d+1) < 1 (Section 5.6).

Quantum error correction lies outside the bound for a different reason. Its exponential, with Λ≈2.14\Lambda \approx 2.14, is error suppression against code distance at a fixed task, not capability against recursive depth, so the bound, an exponent of capability, does not apply to it (Section 5.3).

A ceiling on a class of mechanism: The ARC Bound is a mechanism-class ceiling of the kind thermodynamics made familiar. Just as a heat engine’s maximum efficiency is fixed by its operating temperatures regardless of engineering, on the conjecture no system corrected by mechanisms of its own class would sustain α\alpha above 2, because P6 caps the leverage exponent of such correctors at one half. The analogy holds in the part that matters: a mechanism-class ceiling binds its class, and a device built on a different mechanism is not bound by it at all. Both are ceilings on a class of mechanism, not statements about what is physically possible. Individual systems may fall short due to imperfect coupling, noise, or architectural constraints (the transport comparison of Section 5.6 has different premises and an observable that is not automatically capability), but the ceiling itself is set by the corrector’s class through P6, not by an architecture’s operation count. A system driven above that ceiling does not stay coherent there, so a durably stable measurement above α=2\alpha = 2 would refute the bound under F5, while an unstable excursion would be consistent with it; F11, the earlier criterion, refutes on a sustained magnitude alone. Both are this paper’s own criteria and decide nothing registered: under the registration the bound is refuted only where P6 is, by “a same-class corrector whose measured correction exponent interval lies entirely above one half”. A ceiling of this kind tells us when to stop optimising within a class and when a corrector of a different class is required to exceed it.

Critically, the contradictory evidence reviewed in Section 5.2 (Zeng et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025) may indicate that:

  • α\alpha varies with task difficulty, model architecture, or prompt structure

  • Returns to longer reasoning can stop rising: in Zeng and colleagues’ tests accuracy fell or oscillated with further revisions, and S*’s debugging gains plateaued after two or three rounds

  • Different benchmarks probe different coupling regimes

Resolving these discrepancies is a central empirical question for the Global Scaling Challenge (Section 8).

Caveat. The numerical similarity between the ARC Bound’s α=2\alpha = 2 and Λ≈2.14\Lambda \approx 2.14 (quantum) may be entirely coincidental. These are mathematically distinct quantities from different functional forms. Any deeper connection would require theoretical justification that does not currently exist.

The βL\beta_L-transition phase diagram.

The generalised framework implies a phase diagram of recursive scaling. The axes are base quality (II, normalised) and coupling strength (βL\beta_L). Four regimes emerge:

  • Diminishing returns: βL<βL*\beta_L < \beta_L^* (threshold) or II below threshold. More recursion hurts or provides negligible benefit.

  • Power-law regime: 0.3≲βL≲0.70.3 \lesssim \beta_L \lesssim 0.7, II above threshold. Compounding returns, polynomial scaling. (AI chain-of-thought reasoning.)

  • Near-exponential regime: βL\beta_L close to 1, II well above threshold. The exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) is large, above 10 once βL>0.9\beta_L > 0.9, and growth becomes exponential only in the limit βL=1\beta_L = 1. (Quantum error correction below threshold is drawn here as an analogy: its exponential is the suppression of logical error against code distance at a fixed task, not capability growth.)

  • Saturating regime: Any βL\beta_L with energy dissipation; an approach to a ceiling, whose form the dynamics set (Section 4.1). (Physical oscillators; the time crystal is read as a bounded case, with no growth toward its cycle measured.)

Note: These boundary values are schematic placements, not observations. No βL\beta_L has been measured in the AI results cited here: the early error-decay estimate is retracted, and the surviving fit does not identify βL\beta_L in [0,1)[0,1) or establish its absence. Quantum error correction’s parameter is Λ\Lambda, not βL\beta_L. The precise boundaries require empirical determination via the Global Scaling Challenge.

Cross-domain βL\beta_L prediction: the killer test.

The framework makes a specific, falsifiable cross-domain prediction that distinguishes analogy from unified theory:

The βL\beta_L-Convergence Prediction: In any domain, βL\beta_L can be measured by two independent methods:

  1. From scaling behaviour: On a declared capability metric and resource coordinate, identify the model and its applicable regime before fitting α\alpha and computing βL=1−1/α\beta_L=1-1/\alpha. This is a model-dependent substitution, not an independent coupling measurement; an error-decay fit alone does not license it (Section 5.2.1).

  2. From threshold analysis: Measure the critical coupling βL*\beta_L^* below which recursive gains vanish.

Prediction: These two independent measurements of βL\beta_L will converge to the same value within experimental error.

Cross-domain extension: If we measure βAI\beta_{\text{AI}} from AI scaling data, βQEC\beta_{\text{QEC}} from quantum error correction thresholds, and βbio\beta_{\text{bio}} from metabolic scaling, and these values occupy consistent positions on the βL\beta_L-continuum that correctly predict their respective functional forms, the framework is supported as a unified account. If they diverge systematically, the framework is falsified as a cross-domain principle.

This is the framework’s strongest cross-domain prediction. It transforms the observation that “different domains have different functional forms” into the testable claim that “the same underlying parameter determines all functional forms.”

Concrete Test Protocol:

  1. In quantum error correction: Measure the error suppression factor Λ=pth/pphysical\Lambda = p_{\text{th}}/p_{\text{physical}} directly from logical error rates across code distances. The quantum scaling parameter is Λ\Lambda itself, not derived from βL\beta_L. Quantum error correction is classed as additive composition by analogy, reading code distance as its depth variable, so its exponential lies outside the power-law framework.

  2. In AI systems: Define the capability metric and depth coordinate, and test the applicable growth model. Only if its exponent is identified may βAI=1−1/α\beta_{\text{AI}}=1-1/\alpha be computed as a conditional substitution; a separately measured βL\beta_L is needed to test the identity rather than restate it. Error-decay slopes do not supply that identification.

  3. Cross-domain validation: Verify that quantum error correction follows exponential scaling (εd∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2}) while AI follows power-law scaling (U∝RαU \propto R^{\alpha}). The key structural prediction is that the composition type (additive vs hierarchical) determines the functional form, not a shared numerical parameter.

If the βL\beta_L values from different measurement methods within each domain converge, AND the cross-domain βL\beta_L values correctly predict functional forms, the framework passes its most stringent test. If either condition fails, the framework requires fundamental revision.

Confirmation would establish the ARC Principle as a genuine cross-domain unification. Falsification would reduce it to a collection of domain-specific observations.

Connection to universality theory.

The substrate-independence of the five structural properties is reminiscent of universality in statistical physics, where systems with different microscopic Hamiltonians exhibit identical critical exponents near phase transitions (Wilson 1971). In Wilson’s analysis the exponents are fixed by the renormalisation-group equation rather than by the initial Hamiltonian, so a microscopic detail such as a second-neighbour coupling drops out near criticality.

The ARC framework suggests an analogous phenomenon: near the recursive threshold (the α=1\alpha = 1 boundary), the specific physical substrate may become irrelevant, and only the recursive architecture (structured asymmetry, self-referential coupling, feedback topology) determines scaling behaviour. Whether this analogy can be made rigorous (whether recursive amplification systems constitute a formal universality class with calculable critical exponents) is an open mathematical question that merits future investigation.

The identity is a claim preregistered by timestamp for testing, never an established fact. The stability ceiling and the conversion exponent meet at the same number, and the temptation is to say one constant does two jobs. The claim’s status is stricter: the identity is preregistered by timestamp for testing, in advance of the data, with outcomes that can kill it. Study AE, since withdrawn from the programme, set out the reciprocity requirement between the separately measured leverage cap and stability boundary with three outcomes per cell (supported, refuted, insufficient precision) and an aggregation rule under which one refuted cell refutes the identity. Study AG (Unit 16) measures the coupling and the correction-leverage exponent on one and the same system, each with its own instrument, and tests whether the growth exponent the coupling sustains respects the ceiling the correction-leverage exponent sets. The two derivations share one functional form, so what it tests is their ordering, βL≤χ\beta_L \leq \chi, and it is designed to find a violation. If the channels disagree, the unification is withdrawn from every surface it has reached, with the same prominence as the framing. A match between an asserted one half and the estimated error-decay exponent 0.49 (one model’s inconclusive fit) is not evidence for that identity: the two quantities have not been identified as the same estimand, and a shared number would not provide independent corroboration.

A programme hypothesis beyond the framework. Oversight arrangements that place a human in the loop, as amplification and reinforcement learning from human feedback do, are cross-class by construction, because the human corrector does not share the model’s substrate. The programme therefore hypothesises, beyond what these equations decide, that human-in-the-loop oversight shows a higher correction exponent than pure-model oversight, for a structural reason rather than a sentimental one. The correction exponent belongs to the corrector, and it is a different quantity from the alignment scaling exponent αalign\alpha_{\text{align}} of Section 3.1, which P19 concerns. This is testable on existing data and does not require new systems.

4.6 Composition operator transitions

The framework as presented in Section 4.1 assigns a single composition operator ⊕\oplus to each system. However, computational analysis reveals that this may be an idealisation. In bounded or dissipative systems, the composition operator itself can transition between regimes as recursive depth increases.

The idea came from reading gravitational structure formation in the composition classes, a reading the programme states as an analogy, not a measurement (Eastwood 2026m). On that reading, gravitational collapse passes through three phases:

  1. Inflation/linear growth (read as additive ⊕\oplus): Primordial perturbations grow independently. Each step adds to the previous without cumulative advantage, the exponential (additive Cauchy) form, f(R1+R2)=f(R1)⋅f(R2)f(R_1 + R_2) = f(R_1) \cdot f(R_2), in the reading’s depth variable.

  2. Nonlinear collapse (read as multiplicative ⊕\oplus): Mode coupling emerges; denser regions gravitationally attract more matter, creating cumulative advantage, the power-law form, g(R1⋅R2)=g(R1)⋅g(R2)g(R_1 \cdot R_2) = g(R_1) \cdot g(R_2).

  3. Virialised halos (read as bounded ⊕\oplus): Individual structures reach energy minima. Gains saturate: Qr+1≈QrQ_{r+1} \approx Q_r. The system enters the bounded regime, in which the level holds, as at βL=0\beta_L = 0 in Theorem 1(a).

Computational checks. In logistic growth, gradient descent with momentum and Kuramoto oscillator synchronisation, measuring the local coupling parameter βL\beta_L in sliding windows shows analogous transitions between composition regimes. By contrast, unbounded pure-Bernoulli systems maintain constant βL\beta_L to machine precision (σ<10−6\sigma < 10^{-6}). These are descriptive checks under the chosen estimator; they do not independently establish that the systems change functional-equation class.

Theorem 6 (Composition operator transitions). A single physical system can transition between different composition operator regimes as a function of recursive depth or an internal state parameter. This extends the framework by replacing the assumption of a fixed ⊕\oplus with a depth-dependent ⊕(R)\oplus(R), modelled by extending Axiom 2 to dg/dr=a(g,r)⋅gβL(g,r)dg/dr = a(g, r) \cdot g^{\beta_L(g, r)} where the coupling itself depends on accumulated state.

Why this matters for the contradictory evidence. The finding that different AI studies report conflicting scaling behaviours (Section 5.2) may reflect composition operator transitions rather than genuine contradictions. If reasoning systems begin in an additive regime (shallow thinking, independent steps), transition to multiplicative (deep reasoning with cumulative advantage), and eventually saturate (diminishing returns at extreme depth), then studies measuring at different recursive depths would observe different scaling, even in the same system. The finding of Zeng et al. (2025, arXiv:2502.12215) that accuracy does not rise consistently with chain length, and that correct answers are often shorter, may reflect the transition point between multiplicative and bounded composition.

This interpretation is testable: measure the local coupling parameter βL\beta_L at different reasoning depths within a single AI system. If βL\beta_L is constant, the original framework applies. If βL\beta_L decreases with depth, as the reading of structure formation pictures by analogy, Theorem 6 applies. Either outcome advances understanding of recursive scaling.

Epistemic status: Theorem 6 is a hypothesis drawn from computational examples and stated in the theorem environment for numbering only; it is not a mathematical theorem derivable from the original three axioms. It extends the framework’s scope but requires independent experimental confirmation. The cosmological phases above illustrate the transition; no measurement of an exponent in them is claimed, and the generalisation to AI systems is a prediction, not an established result.

5 The cross-domain evidence

If recursive scaling with α>1\alpha > 1 were specific to AI software, the alignment scaling problem might be an engineering challenge addressable through implementation changes. Systems with no software at all show related structures, with forms that differ. This section sets the framework against them and asks whether recursive amplification could be a structural property of recursive systems rather than a feature of how AI is built; it finds the framework consistent with the independently established forms in three of the four domains.

5.1 Overview

The following table summarises evidence across domains, noting that functional forms differ (see Section 4.1). What unites them is recursive or recurrent processing; the framework is consistent with independently established forms in three of the four domains (biology, quantum error correction and classical time crystals). The cross-domain evidence is consistent with the underlying scaling behaviour being structural, in which case changes confined to safeguards outside the loop would not solve the alignment scaling problem.

Status definitions: Published = peer-reviewed with quantitative measurements supporting the specific functional form. Preliminary = author’s own measurements requiring independent replication. Structural = qualitative mapping without quantitative α\alpha measurement. Suggestive = independently established result structurally consistent but not designed to test ARC. Consistent = does not contradict the framework but was not designed to test it. Retracted = withdrawn by the author, kept on the record with its retraction. Preprint = public but not peer reviewed.

Evidence hierarchy: The evidence base is uneven and we state this explicitly. AI error-decay scaling has one interpretable model fit after the early estimate was retracted: about 0.49 by regression and 0.59 by endpoint estimate, whose bootstrap interval, from −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9, makes it inconclusive, one model’s fit (Gemini 3 Flash); it needs independent replication. Quantum error correction provides a structural parallel with different functional form (exponential rather than power-law). The time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework (Section 5.4), and neuroscience represents a structural prediction derived from the framework, not an independent validation: researchers in those domains did not measure α\alpha or test the ARC equation. Biological scaling observations motivate a separate transport model, whose demand, route and measurement premises must be tested. The fungal fits supply no pooled dimensional verdict, and the leaf-venation comparison F12 remains a candidate test. These domains are presented together to show scope, not to claim equivalent evidential standing.

5.2 AI: sequential versus parallel reasoning

Published sources: DeepSeek-R1 Technical Report (released 20 January 2025; arXiv:2501.12948, 22 January 2025; DeepSeek-AI 2025a); Sharma and Chopra (2025), “The Sequential Edge: Inverse-Entropy Voting Beats Parallel Self-Consistency at Matched Compute” (November 2025, arXiv:2511.02309); Snell et al. (2024), “Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters” (August 2024, arXiv:2408.03314).

What they found: Sharma and Chopra (2025) find sequential reasoning ahead of parallel sampling (independent attempts with majority vote) on mathematical reasoning tasks, and Snell et al. (2024) found sequential revisions narrowly ahead; the DeepSeek-R1 report makes no such comparison. Sharma and Chopra (2025) tested 5 state-of-the-art models across 3 challenging benchmarks (AIME-2024, AIME-2025, GPQA-Diamond) under matched computational budgets: sequential wins in 43/45 configurations (95.6%), with accuracy gains up to 46.7 percentage points (Qwen3-235B on AIME-2025: 76.7% sequential vs 30.0% parallel).

Why sequential wins (per Sharma and Chopra 2025): Sequential reasoning enables three mechanisms unavailable in parallel approaches: (1) iterative error correction where models identify and fix mistakes in subsequent steps, (2) progressive context accumulation where each step builds upon accumulated insights, and (3) answer verification where models validate and refine initial responses. The overall effect is statistically robust (t=4.23t = 4.23, p<0.001p < 0.001, Cohen’s d=0.89d = 0.89), and holds across five open-source models from three families (GPT-OSS, Qwen3 and Kimi-K2).

What the voting result shows: Sharma and Chopra (2025) tested seven different voting methods for aggregating sequential chain outputs. Methods favouring later reasoning steps achieved optimal performance in 97% of configurations (the authors count among them their inverse-entropy weighting, which weights each chain by its confidence), while methods favouring earlier steps (exponential decay) achieved optimality in only 17%. Later steps are therefore more valuable than earlier ones, which any chain that improves step by step would show, whether its returns compound or diminish: the result is consistent with α>1\alpha > 1 and does not distinguish it from α<1\alpha < 1.

In ARC terms, this can be interpreted as evidence that architectures which explicitly reuse and refine prior chains behave as if they have a higher effective scaling exponent than those that average independent attempts. However, Sharma and Chopra (2025) do not fit α\alpha or βL\beta_L directly; this connection is interpretive rather than quantitative.

Author’s estimates (Papers I and II): The early range α≈1.3\alpha\approx1.3 to 2.22.2 described error-decay calculations in the author’s prior work (Eastwood 2026l, 2026c). It was not a measured range of capability-growth or coupling exponents. The upper figure is retracted, and the later multi-model study substantially revised the picture:

  • The error-decay endpoint slope αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} in Paper I, version 1.19, equation (3) and Table 3, is ∼1.34{\sim}1.34 as recorded, and 1.22 to 1.49 under the rounding of the published token averages alone. It is an error-decay estimate on the token axis, not the capability exponent, and uses only two observations: DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-R1-0528, each at its developer-reported average thinking-token use on AIME 2025. The source is the developer’s model card (DeepSeek-AI 2025b); the technical report describes the model (DeepSeek-AI 2025a). Different model versions and token use vary together, so the pair does not isolate a recursion effect or measure βL\beta_L.

  • The error-decay estimate αerr≈2.2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.2 (Paper II, original 12-problem experiment: the DeepSeek R1 run of 21 January 2026) derives from the author’s own AIME experiment with 95% CI 1.5 to 3.0. This does not replicate in the multi-model tier-2 extension, and has since been retracted.

  • Paper II completed results (March 2026; updated v11.0): Extending to five frontier models (those forming the capability arm within a study of six models) across 18 harder tier-2 problems (AIME/Putnam level) produced findings that differed between models in that replication. αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.24 is retracted: it did not reproduce in Paper II’s replication on five frontier models. Gemini 3 Flash provides the cleanest error-decay fit, about 0.49 by regression (r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86) and 0.59 by endpoint estimate, whose bootstrap interval, from −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9, makes it inconclusive. Ceiling effects swallow Grok 4.1 Fast (96.3% to 100% at every depth) and DeepSeek R1, GPT-5.4 produces a binary step function rather than a dependable power law, and Qwen3 sits close to floor. The parallel error-decay exponent is near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), and none for Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100% at every sample count, and the sequential error-decay exponent exceeds the parallel one wherever both could be estimated (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably), at compute that was not matched.

  • Accuracy figures differ slightly across papers due to different data sources, problem sets, and estimation methods

Statistical caveat: The original αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} estimates are from the author’s preliminary work, not from the published sources (DeepSeek-AI 2025a; Sharma and Chopra 2025). Sharma and Chopra (2025) report the directional finding (sequential above parallel); neither source calculates αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} in this form, and that direction is itself contested, since Gu and colleagues (arXiv:2604.05868, April 2026; Gu et al. 2026) report the opposite result, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding. The Paper II multi-model replication (March 2026) did not reproduce the original error-decay estimate αerr≈2.2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.2, which the author has retracted. Gemini 3 Flash gave the only clean error-decay power-law fit among the five capability-arm models, about 0.49 (one model’s inconclusive fit), while the other architectures are dominated by ceiling, floor, or step-function behaviour. The parallel error-decay exponent is near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), and none for Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100% at every sample count.

5.2.1 The metric bridge: error decay and capability growth

Paper II, version 2.19, equation (1), models the proportion of incorrect answers as E(R)=E0R−αerrE(R)=E_0R^{-\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}}, where E0>0E_0>0 and R>0R>0 is its stated resource coordinate (tokens or samples). The endpoint calculation is αerr=ln⁡(E1/E2)/ln⁡(R2/R1)\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}=\ln(E_1/E_2)/\ln(R_2/R_1) for positive errors. This is an error-decay exponent, not an exponent of accuracy and not automatically the capability exponent αcap\alpha_{\text{cap}} in the safety ratio.

If capability is explicitly operationalised as Uinv=K/E(R)U_{\mathrm{inv}}=K/E(R) with a fixed positive constant KK, then the same error power law on the same resource coordinate gives Uinv=(K/E0)RαerrU_{\mathrm{inv}}=(K/E_0)R^{\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}}. This chosen inverse-error proxy has the same numerical exponent. Accuracy 1−E(R)1-E(R) generally does not: its local elasticity is αerrE(R)/(1−E(R))\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}E(R)/(1-E(R)) where 0<E(R)<10<E(R)<1. Measured zero error makes the inverse undefined; a model for error above a nonzero floor must not be substituted for the error itself. Neither the choice of proxy nor an algebraic conversion validates a general capability construct.

The further substitution βL=1−1/α\beta_L=1-1/\alpha needs identification with the growth model g′=agβLg'=ag^{\beta_L} and its coordinate and regime. Its shifted solution is not a pure power of the original depth at finite RR (Appendix A.3); the power law in the shifted clock of Appendix A is a different parameterisation. Thus 0.49 does not independently measure coupling, show that positive coupling is absent, place a fixed-weight model in a physical regime, or decide a capability ceiling. The same conditions govern the error-decay endpoint slope ∼1.34{\sim}1.34 in Paper I. Tokens, samples and completed self-improvement revisions are different resource coordinates; a mapping to the model depth must be justified. The two-version comparison there and the unmatched compute comparison here do not isolate a recursive mechanism.

For the Gemini 3 Flash result, Paper II, version 2.19, Section 5, reports a regression estimate of 0.49 (SE 0.20, r2=0.86r^2=0.86) and an endpoint estimate of 0.59 (bootstrap 95% interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3,2.9]). Both use the three positive-error depth levels; the regression has one residual degree of freedom. The endpoint interval belongs to 0.59. The reported parallel estimates are 0.31 by endpoint and 0.34 by regression. These are the source’s reported summaries, retained without reanalysis.

Snell et al. (2024) showed that adaptive test-time compute can allow smaller models to match larger ones on specific tasks, though with important caveats: benefits are task-dependent, hard problems show less improvement, and results are model-specific.

Contradictory evidence and boundary conditions.

Important: Not all research supports unlimited sequential scaling. Several 2025 studies found conditions where the sequential advantage breaks down:

  • Zeng et al. (2025) (2025, arXiv:2502.12215) found that for o1-like models (QwQ, DeepSeek-R1 and its distilled versions, LIMO), longer chains-of-thought do not consistently enhance accuracy, most markedly in the weaker models. Correct solutions were often shorter than incorrect ones. They found parallel scaling gave better coverage and scalability than sequential scaling, and proposed Shortest Majority Vote, a parallel method favouring shorter solutions, which outperformed standard majority voting, particularly on AIME.

  • Li et al. (2025) (2025, arXiv:2502.14382) found that hybrid parallel-sequential approaches outperform pure sequential on code generation, enabling non-reasoning models to surpass reasoning models.

  • Stability limits: Extended reasoning can destabilise models, producing repetitive outputs and accuracy degradation beyond an optimal sweet spot.

  • Task-type boundary: Sharma and Chopra (2025)’s own creative task ablation provides a useful constraint: on joke generation, parallel approaches achieved greater semantic diversity (broader conceptual exploration) while sequential approaches achieved greater lexical diversity (deeper linguistic refinement). This suggests the sequential advantage applies most strongly to convergent tasks requiring iterative error correction, and may not generalise to divergent tasks requiring breadth of exploration.

  • The acoustic time crystal (no saturation evidence): Morrell, Elliott and Grier’s paper describes every recording it reports as an oscillation already established, and reports no onset. The antisymmetric mode’s coherence time in its second experiment is (100±10)(100 \pm 10) s, about 6,700 cycles, and the authors add: “Sustained oscillations persist for hours longer than the measurement window, which means that the true coherence time of the nonequilibrium steady state may be substantially larger” (Morrell et al. 2026). No growth exponent has been measured in this system, so it gives no evidence on whether systems with α>1\alpha > 1 scale indefinitely.

What this means for the ARC Principle: The comparisons set a concrete task: determine when extra sequential reasoning improves a declared measure at matched compute. Paper II reports one clean error-decay fit, Gemini 3 Flash’s inconclusive 0.49, alongside ceiling, floor and step-function patterns. In that dataset sequential error-decay slopes exceed parallel slopes wherever both can be estimated, with unmatched compute. Whether this pattern persists across architectures and problem sets, and whether any declared capability metric follows the recursive growth model, are separate questions. Identifying the conditions under which a clean power law emerges remains a priority.

Caveat. The contradictory evidence and Paper II results leave the general capability-growth prediction open. The observed ordering is of error-decay slopes at unmatched compute: sequential above parallel where both could be estimated, and parallel below one where estimable. A claim about αcap>1\alpha_{\text{cap}}>1 requires the explicit metric and model identification above, not a relabelling of those slopes.

5.3 Quantum: Google Willow, error correction below the surface code threshold (announced December 2024; preprint public from August 2024)

Source: Acharya, R. et al. [Google Quantum AI] (9 December 2024). “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold.” Nature, 638, 920 to 926 (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024); the team’s preprint was submitted to arXiv on 24 August 2024 and public by 27 August 2024. An Author Correction of 28 April 2026 amends only the labels of its Figure 3a (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2026).

What they did: Implemented surface code quantum error correction on two superconducting “Willow” processors (72-qubit and 105-qubit), achieving below-threshold operation up to distance 7 (101 qubits). Also ran repetition codes to distance 29 over 5.5 hours of processor time (2×10102 \times 10^{10} error correction cycles).

The scaling equation. The fundamental surface code relation is: εd∝(ppthr)(d+1)/2\begin{equation*} \varepsilon_d \propto \left(\frac{p}{p_{\text{thr}}}\right)^{(d+1)/2} \end{equation*}(9) where dd is code distance, pp is physical error rate, pthrp_{\text{thr}} is threshold error rate, and εd\varepsilon_d is logical error rate. The error suppression factor Λ=pthr/p\Lambda = p_{\text{thr}}/p measures how much each increase of two in code distance reduces logical error: Λ=2.14±0.02\Lambda = 2.14 \pm 0.02 with neural network decoding.

The phase transition: direct experimental demonstration. By injecting coherent errors of variable strength (Fig. 2b in the paper), the team swept continuously through the threshold:

Table 8. The regimes above, at and below the surface code threshold in the quantum error-correction experiment of Section 5.3: physical error rate, effect of added code distance and ARC analogue.
Regime Physical error rate Effect of added code distance ARC analogue (a correspondence of structure; no exponent)
Above threshold (p>pthrp > p_{\text{thr}}) High More qubits →\to higher logical error Diminishing returns
At threshold (p=pthrp = p_{\text{thr}}) Critical More qubits →\to no net change Neutral
Below threshold (p<pthrp < p_{\text{thr}}) Low More qubits →\to exponentially lower error Compounding returns

This is, so far as this programme’s search reaches, a direct experimental demonstration of an error-correcting code crossing between regimes where added code distance hurts, is neutral, or helps; read with code distance as its depth variable, by analogy, it has the shape of the qualitative phase transition that the ARC Principle describes. What was measured is logical error against code distance; the table’s last column is a correspondence of structure, and no exponent of capability against depth was measured. The result is graded as convergent timing, never as a prediction, because the team’s preprint of August 2024 was public before the author’s sealed manuscript record of 8 December 2024.

Error budget as decomposition of II. The paper’s error budget for 1/Λ1/\Lambda (its Supplementary Table S6, for the 72-qubit processor with correlated matching) attributes about 60% to errors related to CZ gates (41% to the CZ gates themselves, 11% to CZ crosstalk and 5% to CZ leakage), about 20% to data-qubit idle errors, 12% to readout and reset errors, 9% to single-qubit gate errors and 1% to leakage from heating. This is a decomposition of the system’s base quality, the quantum analogue of ARC’s structured asymmetry term II. Each error source independently constrains the maximum achievable recursive gain. Improving any single component improves Λ\Lambda across all code distances simultaneously: the multiplicative interaction between II and RR that ARC formalises.

Leakage removal as active II-maintenance. Data Qubit Leakage Removal (DQLR), which actively removes accumulated qubit excitations each cycle, produces a 35% increase in Λ\Lambda at distance 5 despite only a 12% reduction in detection probability. Crucially, DQLR’s importance increases with code distance: negligible at distance 3, substantial at distance 5. This demonstrates that maintaining base quality during recursive processing becomes more critical as recursive depth increases, consistent with ARC’s prediction that effective α\alpha depends not just on initial II but on sustained II throughout the recursive chain.

Repetition code error floor: the regime boundary. At high code distances (d≥15d \geq 15), the exponential error suppression deviates from prediction and plateaus at ∼10−10\sim 10^{-10}, caused by rare correlated error bursts (∼\sim30 qubits affected simultaneously, occurring approximately once per hour). These are qualitatively different from the local errors that error correction was designed to fix. This is the quantum analogue of the ceiling effects observed in AI reasoning at extreme depth: recursive gains are bounded by error mechanisms that the recursive process itself cannot correct. The framework describes a regime, not an asymptotic law.

Decoder quality affects scaling. The same quantum hardware achieves different Λ\Lambda depending on decoder quality: neural network decoder Λ=2.18\Lambda = 2.18 vs real-time sparse blossom decoder Λ=2.0\Lambda = 2.0. The “interpreter” of each recursive cycle’s output affects the system’s effective scaling, analogous to how the quality of chain-of-thought reasoning strategies affects effective α\alpha in AI systems.

Stability and robustness. Performance remained stable across 16 runs over 15 hours, with the processor recalibrated between every four runs (average Λ=2.18±0.07\Lambda = 2.18 \pm 0.07). Critically, a fluctuation that affected the worst distance-3 quadrant was suppressed in the distance-5 code, which the authors take to suggest that larger codes are less sensitive to component-level fluctuations; by analogy, deeper recursive systems may be more robust to individual component failures. The distance-7 logical qubit lifetime (291±6291 \pm 6 μ\mus) exceeds the best constituent physical qubit (119±13119 \pm 13 μ\mus) by a factor of 2.4±0.32.4 \pm 0.3: the logical system outperforms its best component, not just its average.

Structural correspondence (what IS shared):

Table 9. The structural correspondence between ARC components and their quantum error-correction analogues, with the measured values.
ARC Component Quantum Analogue Measured
II (base quality / structured asymmetry) Λ=pthr/p\Lambda = p_{\text{thr}}/p (distance from threshold) 2.14±0.022.14 \pm 0.02
RR (recursive depth) (d+1)/2(d+1)/2 (steps of two in code distance) Up to 4 (distance 7)
α>1\alpha > 1 threshold p<pthrp < p_{\text{thr}} boundary Directly measured via error injection
βL\beta_L (self-referential coupling) Per-cycle error suppression efficiency Dependent on decoder quality

Each measured value in the last column is an error-suppression observable of the source; no α\alpha or βL\beta_L of capability against depth is measured, so the first two columns are correspondences of structure.

Critical mathematical distinction. Λ\Lambda and α\alpha describe fundamentally different scaling behaviours:

  • Λ\Lambda parameterises exponential suppression: εd∝Λ−R\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-R} where R=(d+1)/2R = (d+1)/2

  • α\alpha parameterises power-law scaling: U∝RαU \propto R^{\alpha}

As functions of a common mathematical coordinate, an exponential with positive rate eventually exceeds any fixed power. That ordering alone does not rank quantum error correction above AI reasoning: code distance and recursive depth, the observables and the resource costs differ. This paper uses the quantum comparison as an analogy; Λ\Lambda is the source’s measured error-suppression factor, not a capability-growth exponent, as the Foundational Paper also states. The numerical similarity between Λ=2.14\Lambda = 2.14 and the original single-model error-decay estimate αerr≈2.2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.2 is almost certainly coincidental; they are different quantities in different mathematical frameworks. (The αerr≈2.2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.2 estimate, from the DeepSeek R1 run of 21 January 2026, has since been retracted; the best surviving error-decay regression estimate is about 0.49, one model’s inconclusive fit: Section 6.2.)

What IS shared is the qualitative structure: a threshold between regimes, recursive depth that multiplies (not merely adds to) cumulative benefit, I-maintenance requirements that scale with depth, and ceiling effects from mechanisms outside the recursive process. The two forms describe different observables, so neither is a bound on the other.

Why antisymmetric = sequential.

In the antisymmetric mode the pair moves relatively, in a breathing motion; in the symmetric mode it moves jointly. In the source, the quantities Δji(n)=xjn−xin\Delta_{ji}(n) = x_j^n - x_i^n and σji(n)=xjn+xin\sigma_{ji}(n) = x_j^n + x_i^n are differences and sums of powers of the beads’ dimensionless radii, xj=kajx_j = k a_j, which set how strongly, and how nonreciprocally, the beads couple; “[t]he latter of these factors changes sign under exchange of indices and therefore describes a nonreciprocal contribution to the pair interaction” (Morrell et al. 2026). The framework reads the antisymmetric mode, in which each bead’s motion feeds the other’s through that nonreciprocal coupling, as the physical correspondent of output-to-input feedback, and the symmetric mode as the correspondent of parallel processing, independent agents that do not use each other’s outputs as inputs; these are correspondences of structure, and no quantity in the source compounds over cycles in the sense of Section 4.4.

Coherence and saturation.

In Morrell, Elliott and Grier’s second experiment, the antisymmetric mode’s coherence time is (100±10)(100 \pm 10) s, about 6,700 cycles at 66.787 Hz, “comparable to the 108 s duration of the data set”, and the authors add that “[s]ustained oscillations persist for hours longer than the measurement window, which means that the true coherence time of the nonequilibrium steady state may be substantially larger” (Morrell et al. 2026). The oscillation is a linearly stable limit cycle, the time crystal itself: its coherence time is neither a time to reach that cycle, nor a saturation, nor a ceiling on recursion depth. The steady oscillation is nonetheless bounded, which is consistent with reading the ARC equation as describing a scaling regime rather than an unbounded law.

Substrate independence.

The time crystal phenomenon has now been demonstrated in at least two physically distinct substrates:

  • Acoustic (Morrell et al. 2026): Millimetre-scale polymer beads, 40 kHz standing wave

  • Photonic (Raskatla et al. 2024): a continuous space-time crystal state in a photonic metamaterial, driven by nonreciprocal optical forces

The emergence of the same antisymmetric/threshold pattern across different media suggests the underlying structure (nonreciprocal coupling →\to asymmetric mode dominance) may be substrate-independent. Beside the framework’s conjecture that the recursive amplification pattern is architectural rather than implementation-specific, this is a correspondence of structure, not a test of it, since no growth exponent has been measured in a time crystal.

Caveat. No α\alpha has been measured in this system. The mapping is structural, not quantitative. The limit-cycle saturation also implies that any measured α\alpha describes a scaling regime, not unbounded growth. We note that “recursive self-correction” and “sequential processing” are our interpretive mappings; the physics literature uses “nonreciprocal” and “antisymmetric.”

Status of this subsection.

Two forms were set against each other for the oscillation’s growth from rest: the established form and a bare power law. The framework’s composition rule gives the same onset form as the established account of the instability (an exponential onset that settles to a steady oscillation), so the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework, and no study of it is registered. The earlier prediction, a power law with an exponent above one, is withdrawn: it rested on the early estimate of about 2.24, since retracted, and it asked for an analysis the laboratory’s paper does not contain, since Morrell, Elliott and Grier report only steady-state recordings and no onset. Unit 20 (study-t), the acoustic time-crystal form-and-engine analysis designed against the laboratory’s public deposit (Morrell and Grier 2025), is kept as a consistency check, not as a registration. The transient-phase protocol, the physical prediction and the three falsification conditions that version 1.17 printed here are kept whole in Appendix B.13.

5.5 Neuroscience: recurrent processing and the COGITATE collaboration

Sources: Lamme (2006), “Towards a true neural stance on consciousness,” Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 10(11), 494 to 501; Storm, Pennartz et al. (2024), “An integrative, multiscale view on neural theories of consciousness,” Neuron, 112(10), 1531 to 1552; COGITATE Consortium (2025), “Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness,” Nature, 642, 133 to 142; Zheng et al. (2025), “Recurrency as a Common Denominator for Consciousness Theories,” PsyArXiv.

Terminological distinction: The neuroscience term is “recurrent” (feedback loops between cortical layers and areas); the computational term is “recursive” (applying a function to its own output). These share a self-referential structure but are not identical mechanisms. The mapping is structural, not mechanistic.

COGITATE (2025): This adversarial collaboration (a preregistered study of n = 256 across three neuroimaging modalities: iEEG, MEG, fMRI) tested competing predictions of Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNWT) and Integrated Information Theory (IIT) using theory-neutral protocols. Neither theory was fully vindicated:

  • GNWT predictions: Prefrontal regions showed onset responses and a transient categorical representation at stimulus onset, and GNWT’s all-or-none threshold prediction was partly challenged. The predicted PFC ignition at stimulus offset was robustly absent.

  • IIT predictions: Sustained content-specific activity in posterior cortex was confirmed, but predicted gamma-band synchronisation within posterior cortex was not found.

The study reports results that “align with some predictions of IIT and GNWT, while substantially challenging key tenets of both theories”, and highlights “the need for a quantitative framework for systematic theory testing and building”. Critically, the predictions most robustly confirmed (sustained content-specific activity in posterior cortex) are shared by theories emphasising recurrent processing, among them recurrent processing theory (Lamme 2006), as the study names it.

Sustained vs transient processing: COGITATE found that posterior cortex maintained content-specific information throughout stimulus duration (0.5 to 1.5 s), while prefrontal cortex showed only brief categorical responses (∼\sim0.2 to 0.4 s); on this paper’s reading, posterior cortex is characterised by recurrent feedback loops and prefrontal cortex by transient broadcast. Posterior regions carried category and face orientation, and identity for letters and false fonts; PFC carried category, not identity, and orientation only weakly in MEG. This sustained-vs-transient pattern, in which recurrent processing produces richer and more detailed representations than transient broadcast, mirrors the sequential-vs-parallel performance signature found in AI systems (Sharma and Chopra 2025).

Graded cascade model: Separate work by Zheng et al. (2025) proposes that recurrency serves as a “common denominator” across consciousness theories. They describe a “graded cascade” in which deeper recursion expands the set of reportable, behaviour-driving variables, local recurrence carrying phenomenal content and global recurrence access. They argue that recurrency is a shared structural feature across otherwise competing frameworks and a unifying, mechanistic scaffold for consciousness, and they rebut doubts about its sufficiency.

Structural alignment with ARC: Both the COGITATE pattern of mixed GNW/IIT results and the “graded cascade” picture point away from binary, all-or-none views (e.g., a single ignition threshold) and towards graded, multi-stage, feedback-dependent transitions. This is qualitatively similar to ARC’s view that increasing self-referential coupling βL\beta_L moves a system through a continuum of scaling regimes (from linear α=1\alpha = 1 to increasingly super-linear α>1\alpha > 1), rather than a single hard phase transition. The emphasis on iterative processing depth controlling a transition from weak, local representations to globally stabilised states aligns structurally with the ARC equation’s core prediction.

Caveat. COGITATE did not test the ARC framework, did not measure power-law scaling, and did not quantify “depth” of recurrence as a continuous variable. Neither COGITATE nor Zheng et al. (2025) measure α\alpha, βL\beta_L, or any explicit UU vs RR scaling curve. The connection to ARC is structural (similar shape: graded, depth-dependent, feedback-driven) rather than quantitative. “Recurrent” and “recursive” are related but distinct mechanisms. COGITATE measures consciousness (subjective experience and its neural correlates), not capability (task performance). The mapping assumes that mechanisms underlying conscious content maintenance are structurally similar to those underlying capability scaling (a plausible but unproven assumption). What COGITATE does constrain is GNWT’s prediction of ignition at stimulus offset, which was absent, and IIT’s prediction of sustained synchronisation within posterior cortex, which was not found. A terminology note: IIT’s scalar Φ\Phi is a different object from the Φ(H,χ)\Phi(H, \chi) functional appearing in this programme’s December 2024 formalism; the two share only a symbol.

5.6 Biology: conditional transport scaling and source-specific measurements

Sources: West, G.B., Brown, J.H. & Enquist, B.J. (1997). ‘A general model for the origin of allometric scaling laws in biology.’ Science, 276, 122 to 126 (West et al. 1997). Kleiber, M. (1932). ‘Body size and metabolism.’ Hilgardia, 6, 315 to 353 (Kleiber 1932). Eastwood, M.D. (2026). ‘On the Origin of Scaling Laws: what can composition and transport explain?’ (Eastwood 2026i).

The conditional transport result. The formula d/(d+1)d/(d+1) does not follow from spatial dimension or Cauchy’s equation alone. The transport accounts cited here (West et al. 1997, 1999; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010) rest on premises of their own about the network; the other derivations previously compared (Demetrius 2003; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013) must be read under their own models. On the Origin of Scaling Laws, version 3.15 (revised 9 November 2026), Sections 6 and 10, states one explicit route. On a rooted tree with source-to-sink demands qi≥0q_i\geq0, total throughput B=∑iqi>0B=\sum_iq_i>0, edge lengths ℓe\ell_e and flows QeQ_e equal to the demands downstream of each edge, with no unaccounted loss or creation along the routes, the transport quantity is Ctr=∑eℓeQe=Bℓ‾qC_{\mathrm{tr}}=\sum_e\ell_eQ_e=B\bar\ell_q, where ℓ‾q\bar\ell_q is the flow-weighted mean route length. It has units of demand rate times length; it is not automatically body mass or energy cost. Recirculating flows require separate accounting.

For a family with linear scale LL, suppose B∼b0LμB\sim b_0L^\mu and ℓ‾q∼ℓ0Lζ\bar\ell_q\sim\ell_0L^\zeta, with positive constants and μ>0\mu>0. Then BB scales against CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}} with exponent αC=μ/(μ+ζ)\alpha_C=\mu/(\mu+\zeta) where μ+ζ>0\mu+\zeta>0. Demand at macroscopic distance gives ζ≥1\zeta\geq1 only if a fixed positive fraction of demand remains at distances proportional to LL. The equality μ=d\mu=d additionally needs sink number proportional to LdL^d and asymptotically constant mean demand. Bounded route stretch then gives ζ=1\zeta=1. These are the premises behind αC=d/(d+1)\alpha_C=d/(d+1) in this route.

To read that throughput exponent as a metabolic-rate/body-mass exponent requires a measurement bridge. If M∼m0CtrηM\sim m_0C_{\mathrm{tr}}^\eta with η>0\eta>0, the exponent is αC/η\alpha_C/\eta; it equals αC\alpha_C only for the corresponding linear bridge. Cauchy’s scale-invariance result selects a power-law form under its assumptions, not these transport parameters or the observable.

The biological interpretation remains contested. White and Seymour (2003) reports a two-thirds rather than three-quarters account under stated metabolic measurement conditions, and Kozłowski and Konarzewski (2004, 2005) question the network account as well as its mathematics. Neither the exponent nor the mechanism is established merely by an organism’s dimensional label. A comparison must identify its measured variables and test the transport and measurement premises rather than presume them.

The following formula is the conditional value for αC\alpha_C under the premises just stated; the legacy symbol α\alpha in equation (10) is read in that scope: α=dd+1\begin{equation*} \alpha = \frac{d}{d + 1} \end{equation*}(10)

For finite positive dd, d/(d+1)<1d/(d+1)<1 is an algebraic fact about that formula. It is not a universal bound on every observable of a finite-dimensional system. Transferring it to metabolism needs the demand, route-length and mass bridge above. The super-linear metabolic and urban quantities reported by DeLong et al. (2010; Bettencourt et al. 2007) do not contradict finite-dimensional geometry; they concern different observable pairs and mechanisms.

What the fungal source reports.

Aguilar-Trigueros et al. (2017), Table 1 at 20 degrees Celsius, gives the three fits in Table 13. The first two pair colony respiration with biomass; Figure 1c identifies the third as specific metabolic rate against radial extension. These are colony comparisons, not isolated-hypha measurements.

Group nn bb SE PP

Saprotrophic 5 0.53 0.07 8.96×10−38.96\times10^{-3}

The source’s n=24n=24 includes genotypes. Its body and table differ on the third PP; this paper reports Table 1 explicitly. Narrow ranges, differing growing conditions and unclear active versus endogenous metabolism limit comparison (Aguilar-Trigueros et al. 2017). No pooled mean, one-sample test, equivalence claim or discrimination among network dimensions is made from these heterogeneous slopes. The old pooled values, percentage errors, p-values and dimensional-ladder figure are retained only in the labelled history (Appendix B.7).

The former dimensional-ladder figure is reproduced as superseded history in Appendix B.7; it carries no active evidential weight.

What dimensional comparisons can establish. One half, two thirds and three quarters are the values of d/(d+1)d/(d+1) at d=1,2,3d=1,2,3. A valid comparison must independently establish the transport model and observable bridge; selecting a dimension because an observed exponent is nearby is not a test. The vascular and transport models of West et al. (1997, 1999; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010) motivate specific hypotheses. Neither the Cauchy classification nor the presence of a network proves a common exponent or mechanism across those hypotheses.

Geometry and transport cost are different quantities.

The earlier thermodynamic-drag account and its replacement by an unconditional geometric necessity both exceeded the model stated here. Geometry constrains route lengths under specified demand assumptions; energy expenditure requires further constitutive information. The result d/(d+1)<1d/(d+1)<1 does not follow for every biological response merely from a body’s dimension.

The safety question uses a different observable. Metabolic rate against body mass, throughput against transport quantity and capability against recursive depth are distinct relationships. Neither a conditional transport exponent nor a fungal colony’s shape fixes the capability exponent of an AI system. Under the stated recursive model, 0<βL<10<\beta_L<1 gives α=1/(1−βL)>1\alpha=1/(1-\beta_L)>1; its application still needs measurement. A value above one for that observable would not violate a universal geometric bound, because no such universal bound is established here.

Caveat. Kleiber’s metabolic exponent remains contested (Glazier 2005). Network dimension alone supplies neither a metabolic exponent nor an explanation of its variation. A test of the conditional transport model must specify throughput, demands, route lengths and the bridge to the measured biological variable. Fungal colony fits and failed rejection of a selected fraction are not substitutes for that test.

5.7 Substrate-dependent scaling: a unified taxonomy

The cross-domain comparison (Sections 5.2 to 5.6) places two specified mathematical models alongside one another. These are different mechanisms and observable pairs, not an exhaustive partition of physical systems or architectures.
