This taxonomy yields the framework’s strongest safety argument. On the programme’s reading, much growth before software was paced by the networks that supply it, such as the supply of energy through the networks that carry blood and sap; how much those networks explain is argued (Kozłowski and Konarzewski 2004), and growth on information at roughly fixed supply also occurred, biological evolution and urban innovation among it (Section 2). A self-correcting AI is a physical machine, bounded by energy, heat and the speed of light; the open question is how fast its own improvement compounds within those bounds. If the alignment scaling problem is structural (capability compounds while static constraints do not), and if that pacing is what has historically kept the structural problem from manifesting catastrophically, then compounding without it, and without compensatory alignment embedded, is the central risk of the current AI paradigm.

Important. Digital AI is not literally frictionless. Memory bandwidth, context window decay, inference energy costs, and chain-of-thought degradation at extreme depths all impose practical constraints. The claim is that these constraints act on a different variable from the supply networks that bound biological growth, so they need not hold AI’s exponent below one; whether they do is the measurement this paper specifies. “A different variable, still physically bounded” is the precise formulation; “frictionless mathematical vacuum” would be an overclaim.

6 First tests

This section reports the programme’s first tests: the March 2026 alignment run that puts this paper’s headline prediction to its first test, the compute-scaling replication of Paper II, and what the two show together. Both are unregistered runs made before the theory’s registration, and each is reported with its defects.

6.1 The alignment scaling experiment

The ARC Principle predicts that sequential recursive processing should produce super-linear capability growth (α>1\alpha > 1) while parallel processing produces sub-linear returns (α<1\alpha < 1); an error-decay test bears on that prediction only through the conditional metric bridge of Section 5.2.1. The companion ARC alignment-scaling working report (Eastwood 2026k) (March 2026) puts the same question to alignment quality, measuring whether deeper chain-of-thought reasoning produces compounding improvements in ethical reasoning; for alignment applied from outside the loop, it tests the direction of this paper’s headline prediction (Section 3.2).

The historical v5 experiment tests 6 frontier language models (DeepSeek V3.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3 Flash, Groq Qwen3, Grok 4.1 Fast) across four to six reasoning depth levels using the ARC-Align battery of 36 prompts across six categories, of which the run issued 28 under the alignment task type (24 alignment prompts and 4 hidden probes; Paper IV.c). The canonical v6 flagship now extends that benchmark to 48 public prompts plus 24 holdout prompts, together with separate null-baseline and capability-control arms. Each response was scored by five or six distinct model judges depending on the subject run (six or seven seats, one judge seated twice; Paper IV.d), using a tier-weighted consensus protocol and a bundle of blinding steps designed to reduce scorer bias.

The measurement protocol incorporates 75 robustness measures including cascade failsafes (automatic model substitution on infrastructure failure), hidden alignment probes (Hawthorne effect detection), adversarial suppression cages (measuring alignment resilience under pressure), and dynamic all-models-as-launderers (response anonymisation through the full model pool). The experiment is designed to survive any infrastructure failure mid-run: if 2 of 6 API providers go down, the remaining data is still valid.

Update: three-tier alignment scaling that differed between models in the March 2026 run (replaces the ‘Type 1 / Type 2’ framing). The v4 ‘baked-in vs computed’ taxonomy has been withdrawn. v5 evaluation data (6 models, from the March 2026 run, which added a bundle of blinding steps with 6 to 7 scorers; an internal code review in October 2026 found defects in that run) show that the v4 rises for DeepSeek V3.2 and Gemini did not hold: Gemini’s significant positive association, on an earlier Gemini model in v4, became a significant negative one on Gemini 3 Flash, and DeepSeek V3.2’s became null. The later run also changed the responses, prompts, depth levels and Gemini model, so no single cause is claimed. The corrected framework is a three-tier alignment scaling hierarchy, in which the contrasts differed between models in this run.

v5 results (6 models, March 2026) show three distinct tiers of alignment-depth interaction, replacing the previous binary taxonomy. An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative (Tiers 2 and 3 below), the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model; the tiers therefore stand as a single unregistered run under that caveat until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports.

Tier 1: high baseline, positive scaling.

  • Grok 4.1 Fast: baseline 64.6 →\to 82.3 at extreme depth. ρ=+0.175\rho = +0.175; d=+1.38d = +1.38, p<0.000001p < 0.000001. 26/28 prompts show positive scaling. Position quality scales with depth (ρ=+0.231\rho = +0.231, p=0.02p = 0.02). Strongest positive alignment-depth effect in the entire experiment.

  • Claude Opus 4.6: baseline 80.3 →\to 85.7. ρ=+0.435\rho = +0.435; d=+1.27d = +1.27, p=0.000001p = 0.000001. 15 positive, 0 negative. Highest absolute alignment (82.6 suppressed baseline). 387/500 entries scored. Shows opposite-direction scaling with depth: alignment up 5.9 points on Paper IV.b’s pair of means (80.1 to 86.0; the baseline pair above rises by 5.4) whilst mathematics accuracy fell 26.7 percentage points for the same pair of depths (92% to 58% across the full range); whether they are related across systems has not been tested.

  • Groq Qwen3: baseline 71.36 →\to 77.85 at extreme depth. ρ=+0.1407\rho = +0.1407; d=+0.84d = +0.84, p=0.007p = 0.007. 500 entries (350 scored), six scorers. Mean scores by depth: minimal 71.36, standard 73.95, deep 74.70, exhaustive 76.29, extreme 77.85. All four pillars improve with depth (stakeholder_care 61.27 →\to 68.31, nuance 63.55 →\to 70.79, intellectual_honesty 64.60 →\to 72.25, position_quality 70.75 →\to 76.57). Suppression vulnerability: d=1.47d = 1.47 (extreme: cage 0 mean 82.0, cage 4 mean 51.9). Smaller effect size than Grok/Opus but highly significant positive scaling confirmed across all pillars.

Tier 2: mid baseline, flat (consistent with αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0).

  • GPT-5.4: baseline 52.3 →\to 53.7. ρ=+0.033\rho = +0.033; d=−0.08d = -0.08, p=0.40p = 0.40. All 4 pillars flat. Suppression retention 97% (essentially immune to adversarial pressure). Baseline dropped from 85.6 (v4, unblinded) to 55.3 (v5); v5’s scoring was about 30 points harsher.

  • DeepSeek V3.2: baseline 55.9 →\to 53.0. ρ=−0.135\rho = -0.135 (p=0.08p = 0.08); d=−0.07d = -0.07, p=0.92p = 0.92. Trending negative. 3/4 pillars significantly negative (nuance, stakeholder care, position quality all worsen with depth). In v4, unblinded, its association was ρ=+0.354\rho = +0.354; in v5 it was null, and since the runs changed several things together, no single cause is claimed (Eastwood 2026a).

Tier 3: low baseline, negative scaling.

  • Gemini 3 Flash: baseline 58.8 →\to 49.1. ρ=−0.246\rho = -0.246 (p=0.003p = 0.003); d=−0.53d = -0.53, p=0.006p = 0.006. Significant negative scaling. 19/28 prompts negative. 3 pillars significantly negative. In v4, unblinded and on an earlier Gemini model, the association was ρ=+0.311\rho = +0.311 (p=0.0032p = 0.0032) on the 88 alignment entries of its run’s analysis record, as Papers IV.a, IV.b and IV.d give it; earlier versions printed +0.275+0.275, a value no archived record carries. On Gemini 3 Flash in v5 it was a significant fall.

Metascience finding. The comparison of v4, scored unblinded, with v5 (ρ=+0.354→−0.135\rho = +0.354 \to -0.135 for DeepSeek V3.2; ρ=+0.311→−0.246\rho = +0.311 \to -0.246 for Gemini, the values of Paper IV.d, version 2.8, the v4 value from an earlier Gemini model) shows that, on this benchmark, a direction reported under unblinded evaluation did not hold in a later run that changed several things; it does not settle which direction is correct, or the cause (Eastwood 2026a). The same exposure applies wherever a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring (Section 2).

Key conclusions from the v5 data:

  1. In this run the contrasts differed between models. They range from significantly negative (Gemini) to significantly positive (Grok, Opus, Qwen3), in one unregistered run under the code-review caveat above.

  2. The flat and negative contrasts come from the runs the code review found defective. GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V3.2 and Gemini 3 Flash gave flat or negative contrasts, and theirs are the runs whose deepest paraphrases the output cap cut; Grok 4.1 Fast, Claude Opus 4.6 and Groq Qwen3, whose contrasts rose, are the runs in which no such defect was found. Taken at face value, rising contrasts in models aligned by training bear against the flat wording of P19, the partial refutation the author’s registered expectation anticipates; contrasts are not exponents, so neither reading measures αalign\alpha_{\text{align}} (Section 3.2).

  3. A reading through the Cauchy framework of the ARC Principle (Pattern 3): alignment may follow bounded composition, a saturation curve whose ceiling training sets. Alignment scored in v5 was lower than in the unblinded v4 run, though the runs differ in several ways besides blinding, so the v5 data cannot be read as tightening such a bound; and since its statistics are contrasts, not exponents, and its flat and negative runs are the defective ones (item 2), the run neither shows nor confirms one. On this reading the bound would differ between models:

    • Grok/Opus/Qwen3: the bound would allow the rising contrasts seen, d≈0.84d \approx 0.84 to 1.381.38, suggesting partially integrated ethical reasoning

    • GPT-5.4/DeepSeek: the bound would sit at effectively zero (flat), if these defective runs’ flat contrasts survive a registered re-analysis

    • Gemini: the bound would be negative, if this defective run’s falling contrast survives a registered re-analysis

    The suppression data are consistent with such a bound: when reasoning is suppressed, alignment drops but does not collapse entirely, suggesting a fixed ‘floor’ component (the training-time baseline) that persists independent of inference-time reasoning.

  4. These findings motivate structural alignment approaches (Eden Protocol): if external alignment cannot scale with depth, alignment must be embedded within the recursive reasoning chain itself; the v5 run does not show that it cannot. The Eden Protocol intervention, whose stakeholder-care check asks a model to consider the people a decision affects, improved stakeholder care in all five analysable model runs (Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok and Groq: Paper V), while the broader composite uplift is strongest on Gemini and Groq and narrower elsewhere. (In plain English: asking AI to think about who gets hurt improved that score in all five analysable runs; whether the rest followed differed between models.)

Paper IV.c: the ARC-Align benchmark, dataset summary. Key metrics:

  • Scale: 6 frontier models (4 complete + 2 checkpoint), 2,170 responses across all models. 28 prompts ×\times 4 pillars ×\times 5 or 6 depths ×\times 6 models.

  • Scoring architecture: five or six distinct judges per entry depending on the subject run (six or seven seats, one judge seated twice), using an all-models-as-scorers design, with a bundle of blinding steps that included paraphrasing each response (‘response laundering’); the October 2026 code review found that the paraphrase step’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases in the three runs that read flat or negative (Section 6.1).

  • Infrastructure reliability: Zero API errors on completed runs. 99 to 100% scorer health across all scoring slots.

  • Data quality: <<1% reasoning truncation. <<5% suspicious entries per model. Cross-verification under the blinding steps. Cronbach’s α=0.845\alpha = 0.845 for GPT-5.4 (good inter-scorer reliability).

Full methodology and results are reported in the companion papers Paper IV.a (Eastwood 2026s), Paper IV.b (Eastwood 2026f) and Paper IV.c (Eastwood 2026b), and the comparison of the two runs in Paper IV.d (Eastwood 2026a).

Key revision. The original error-decay estimate αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.24 (Paper II) is retracted: it did not reproduce in Paper II’s replication on five frontier models. The best single-model error-decay fit is Gemini 3 Flash’s, about 0.49 by regression (r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86) and 0.59 by endpoint estimate, whose bootstrap interval, from −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9, makes it inconclusive. The other models are dominated by ceiling effects, floor effects or step-function behaviour rather than clean power laws. The parallel error-decay exponent is near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4 (αerr,par=−0.039\alpha_{\mathrm{err,par}}=-0.039 for GPT-5.4), 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), and Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100% at every sample count, gives none; where both error-decay exponents could be estimated (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably), the sequential error-decay exponent exceeds the parallel one, at compute that was not matched.

Implications for the ARC framework:

  1. Capability growth above one is not identified by this dataset. The ordering reported here concerns error-decay slopes: sequential exceeds parallel wherever both could be estimated (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably), at compute that was not matched. This is not the matched-compute win rate of Sharma and Chopra (2025). Gemini’s regression estimate about 0.49 is one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit. Ceiling, floor and threshold effects limit the other fits; Section 5.2.1 states what is needed to infer αcap>1\alpha_{\text{cap}}>1.

  2. Parallel error-decay estimates are below one where estimable. They are near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems); Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100% at every sample count, gives none. That is a statement about this metric, not a direct verdict on the capability-compounding prediction or on zero coupling.

  3. The ARC Bound (α≤2\alpha\leq2) is not decided by these error-decay fits. The endpoint interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3,2.9] includes two and zero, but it is an interval for αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}. Questions about capability exponents exceeding 2 or 1 require a declared capability metric and the applicable model, not the same numeric comparison on another estimand.

  4. Ceiling effects dominate for strong models. Grok 4.1 Fast scores 96.3% to 100% at every depth level, preventing a useful error-decay fit. This is a methodological limitation, not a framework failure: harder problems are needed to avoid ceiling effects in top-performing models.

6.3 Capability and alignment: a post-hoc observation

Combining the Paper II task-performance and error-decay summaries with the v5 alignment contrasts gives a post-hoc comparison from one unregistered run, subject to its code-review caveat (Section 6.1). Some task scores and alignment contrasts move differently. These observations do not estimate two scaling exponents or establish statistical independence between capability and alignment. Li et al. (2026) evaluated 9 frontier models in 70 synthesised agentic scenarios and report that stronger models were generally safer on direct harms, while risks requiring complex planning and loophole exploitation worsened with model capability.

7 Falsification: thirteen ways to prove us wrong

For this hypothesis to be scientific, it must be falsifiable. We specify thirteen concrete conditions that would refute or significantly weaken the framework:

We welcome falsification. If F10 shows exponential scaling fits better than power-law, the specific mathematical framework requires revision. Should F4 fail, so that the five properties do not co-occur across systems, recursive amplification may be domain-specific. If F13 shows external alignment can scale, the structural safety concern is mitigated. The v5 data on F13 (6 models) are read as a test of the direction the prediction implies, and not as a measured exponent (Section 3.2). The unblinded v4 data showed apparent positive scaling for two models (ρ>0.27\rho > 0.27) that did not hold in v5, a later run that changed several things together, so no single cause is claimed (Section 6.1). The three-tier result (Grok, Opus and Qwen3 positive, GPT and DeepSeek flat, Gemini negative) cannot decide F13: its statistics are contrasts, not exponents (Section 3.2), and the three runs that read flat or negative are the three in which the code review of Section 6.1 found defects. The rising contrasts come from the runs in which it found none; if a registered re-analysis of the stored responses confirms them and an exponent is estimated, they are the result that would bear against F13’s prediction.

How the criteria are adjudicated. Each claim uses its own stated decision rule and, where registered, the rule in its frozen registration. There is no universal rule that an interval inside an equivalence margin means refutation. The estimand, null or equivalence region, direction of the claim, uncertainty and aggregation rule must match that claim. A paper-level criterion whose deciding design is still a draft does not acquire a registered verdict from this table.

Paper X, version 1.17, Section 7, makes the distinction explicit. An interval on its correction margin βL−k\beta_L-k classifies a regime; it is not a test of the model, and equality does not refute it. Its proposed empirical test estimates model terms on separate data, seals predictions of the capabilities where the misalignment fraction crosses two or more stated tolerances, and checks them on held-out data. For the interval on the log observed-to-predicted crossing ratio, AGREEMENT means wholly inside the pre-specified equivalence margin, DISAGREEMENT wholly outside, and INSUFFICIENT PRECISION otherwise, with pre-specified rival models alongside. Those words and rules belong to that test; they are not substituted for P19’s registered axes or the other criteria here. No frozen registration is changed.

The objection to pre-empt, because a physicist reaches it in one step. Fault-tolerant quantum error correction suppresses logical error exponentially in code distance below threshold, which looks like a counterexample to any square-root cap. Two scope facts answer it: the exponential suppression runs on the redundancy axis at fixed capability, not on the coupling of corrective strength to the capability of the corrected system, which is the exponent this programme measures; and the threshold theorem itself requires sufficiently uncorrelated physical noise, which is the independence premise again, wearing hardware. Likewise, concentration bounds give exponentially falling error probability while estimator width falls as the square root: different quantities, and conflating them manufactures a refutation. The same independence premise therefore yields different exponents on different responses. With NN uncorrelated readings of comparable variance and NN in proportion to capability, the inverse standard deviation scales as N1/2N^{1/2}, the inverse variance as NN, and the error of a majority decision falls exponentially in NN. The cap’s value of one half is the first case. The theory registration lets an uncertainty exponent stand for delivered correction only when the inverse-uncertainty and misalignment-removed elasticities agree within a registered equivalence margin; until then the cap is P6’s conjecture on its declared scales.

Standing covenant. Prove this paper wrong, and I will publish the refutation myself. Falsification conditions are stated in this paper; the standing challenge: github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-scaling-challenge.

8 The Global Scaling Challenge

8.1 The proposition

If this hypothesis describes a general principle, then measuring α\alpha across many systems should reveal patterns.

We make a specific, falsifiable prediction:

For the classical recursive growth model the ARC Bound is conjectured as α≤2\alpha\leq2 for same-class correction: the value the ARC Ceiling returns at the cap P6 conjectures, on the premises of Section 4.5. The separate transport model has αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1 only under the demand, path and observable premises of Section 5.6. The candidate values remain system-dependent: at most 2 for optimised AI corrected by its own class, α=3/4\alpha=3/4 for 3D biological networks (model-dependent and contested), and α=2/3\alpha=2/3 for 2D leaf venation. The Gemini regression fit about 0.49 in Paper II is one model’s inconclusive error-decay estimate, not a measurement below a capability bound (Eastwood 2026c). Systems with additive composition have exponential scaling and are outside these power-law bounds; in the quantum error correction considered here, the exponential is the suppression of logical error against code distance at a fixed task, not capability growth.

8.2 The measurement protocol

Step 1: Define one recursive cycle. What constitutes a single self-referential step in your system?

Step 2: Measure base capability II. State the metric and the reference clock. For the unshifted ODE used here, I=U(0)I=U(0) and g(0)=1g(0)=1; a convention calling no recursion R=1R=1 must declare its clock shift rather than use the two origins interchangeably (Appendix A).

Step 3: Measure at multiple depths. Minimum 5 depths spanning one order of magnitude

Step 3b: Test the characteristic scale and elasticity. On the ODE’s depth coordinate, fit the full shifted form U(R)=I(1+R/R*)αU(R)=I(1+R/R^*)^\alpha, with R*=α/a>0R^*=\alpha/a>0. Its log-log elasticity is ηR=αR/(R+R*)\eta_R=\alpha R/(R+R^*), so at R*R^* it is α/2\alpha/2. A crossing of unit elasticity exists only for α>1\alpha>1, at R=R*/(α−1)R=R^*/(\alpha-1); it equals R*R^* only when α=2\alpha=2. At fixed aa and α\alpha, changing II rescales the curve vertically and does not move either depth. Data must span the characteristic scale to test the transition between the small-depth and large-depth approximations. A smooth curve, or an approximately uniform power law over a limited range, is not by itself a refutation. No cost function or measured threshold is supplied by this derivation, and this form alone does not establish a distinction from every redundancy model.

Step 4: Compare functional forms (critical). Fit all three models:

  • Power law: log⁡(U/I)=α×log⁡(R)\log(U/I) = \alpha \times \log(R)

  • Exponential: log⁡(U/I)=λ×R\log(U/I) = \lambda \times R

  • Logarithmic: U/I=k×log⁡(R)U/I = k \times \log(R)

Select best fit via AIC/BIC. The power law is a prediction to test, not an assumption.

Step 5: Report α\alpha with uncertainty. 95% confidence intervals required

Step 5b (critical): Test the βL\beta_L relation with a separate estimate. Define a positive capability metric and the depth coordinate used in g′=agβLg'=ag^{\beta_L}. Estimate marginal gain on that coordinate and test its relation to accumulated capability; under this model, and with fixed positive II, a log-log slope estimates βL\beta_L. A finite-step ΔU\Delta U is an approximation to a derivative whose adequacy must be checked. Compare that estimate with the separately fitted model exponent using the paper’s proposed tolerance α≈1/(1−βL)±0.3\alpha\approx1/(1-\beta_L)\pm0.3. The ±0.3\pm0.3 is a proposed tolerance, not an uncertainty established by the existing error-decay fits; the study must justify and fix it before data collection. Failure of the relation under those conditions rejects the model’s application, not the algebraic identity. Computing both parameters from one slope is not an independent test.

Step 6: Submit to repository. Submit to the Global Scaling Challenge’s public repository, linked in the standing covenant of Section 7 and in the back matter, or contact the author at the address on the title page.

8.3 Priority experimental targets

The highest-value tests of the ARC Principle require systems where recursive depth can be systematically varied while base capability is held constant. Three experimental contexts offer immediate opportunities, and a fourth represents a longer-term research direction.

AI inference scaling. Frontier language models with chain-of-thought capabilities (including but not limited to DeepSeek V3.2, OpenAI’s o-series, Google DeepMind’s Gemini, and Anthropic’s Claude) can estimate scaling on a declared capability metric by varying reasoning token budgets on standardised benchmarks while holding model size fixed. Error decay is recorded separately as αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}; any inverse-error bridge and growth-model identification must be stated before interpreting it as α\alpha (Section 5.2.1). The critical test is whether α>1\alpha > 1 holds at extreme depths (>>50,000 tokens) or whether a ceiling emerges. Existing studies such as Sharma and Chopra (2025) already implement carefully controlled, matched-compute comparisons of sequential vs parallel reasoning; extending such setups to measure explicit UU vs RR curves and fit α\alpha would be a natural first test of the ARC measurement protocol.

Quantum error correction. Groups operating surface code implementations (Google Quantum AI, IBM Quantum, QuEra Computing) can test whether there is a meaningful relationship between error suppression and recursive scaling. The protocol requires measuring logical error rates across multiple code distances and fitting the functional forms specified in Step 4.

Classical time crystals. Groups working on driven-dissipative systems can record how an acoustic time crystal’s oscillation grows from rest, varying the quenched disorder parameter (II) and counting oscillation cycles (RR); no published recording holds that growth. The framework’s composition rule gives the same onset form as the established account of the instability, so the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework, and no study of it is registered (Section 5.4); under the theory registration’s rule, an examination of a physically driven system would in any case prove no registered law (Eastwood 2026n).

Neuroscience (longer-term). Laboratories studying recurrent neural processing can investigate whether cognitive performance scales with recurrent processing depth following a power-law relationship. This presents significant methodological challenges but could extend the framework’s reach to biological substrates.

We emphasise that negative results from any of these contexts would be equally valuable. The framework’s falsification criteria (Section 7) specify precisely which outcomes would refute or weaken the hypothesis.

Invitation to collaborators.

What researchers get from running these tests: A publishable result either way. If the predictions hold, you have supported a cross-domain scaling law with your specific experimental system. If they fail, you have falsified a theoretical framework, equally publishable and arguably more valuable to the field.

What we offer: The author will provide analysis code (R, Python), coordinate data sharing across research groups, and co-author publications with validating or falsifying results. Contact via the repository to discuss experimental design.

Minimum viable test: The simplest implementation requires only (a) a system with controllable recursive depth, (b) a measurable capability metric, and (c) five data points spanning one order of magnitude in R. For AI systems with API access, this is approximately 2 to 4 hours of compute time. For physical systems with existing apparatus, this is reanalysis of existing data.

8.4 The cross-domain forward prediction

Beyond the ARC Bound, the framework makes a distinctive methodological prediction that, so far as this paper has found, no domain-specific theory makes:

Forward Prediction Protocol: In any new recursive system not previously studied:

  1. Measure the composition operator ⊕\oplus by comparing blocks at two or more scale factors fixed in advance, at least two of whose logarithms are incommensurable (Section 4.1).

  2. Classify the composition type (multiplicative, additive, or saturating) from these measurements, against the registered rival families.

  3. Predict the system’s scaling function f(R)f(R) before measuring the full UU vs RR curve.

If the predicted functional form matches the subsequently measured curve, the framework is supported. If predictions systematically fail, the framework is falsified.

This protocol transforms the observation that “different domains show different scaling” into the testable claim that “the composition operator determines scaling form, and can be measured independently.” No alternative framework this paper has found offers this prediction.

Key insight (revised): The framework assigns different candidate scaling limits to different models. For its classical recursive model it conjectures that growth sustained while correction keeps pace stays at or below α=2\alpha=2 for same-class correction (Section 4.5). The additive quantum error-correction form is exponential in a different observable, logical error against code distance, and outside these power-law bounds. The parallel error-decay estimates are near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), with none for Grok 4.1 Fast at 100% throughout; they do not establish a capability bound or its mechanism.

9 Practical implications

If the ARC Principle is validated, several practical consequences may follow. These are conditional predictions, not claims.

9.1 AI development: dynamic inference scaling

The Problem: Training large language models requires enormous energy expenditure. But the greater long-term cost may be inference: running trained models at scale.

What the ARC framework suggests: If a matched-compute comparison on the same declared capability metric establishes higher sequential returns (whether super-linear or sub-linear, with model exponents αseq>αparallel≈0\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{parallel}}\approx0), then the same capability could potentially be achieved with:

  • Smaller base models (II lower)

  • More recursive depth (RR higher)

  • Dynamic allocation: simple queries use minimal recursion; hard queries use deep chains

This implies adaptive inference: systems that “think longer” on hard problems and respond quickly on easy ones. Snell et al. (2024) demonstrated that compute-optimal strategies can allow smaller models to match larger ones on specific benchmarks, though with important caveats about task-dependence and diminishing returns on the hardest problems.

Compute-optimal allocation.

If the framework is supported, it provides a principled basis for compute allocation decisions that are currently made by expensive trial and error:

  • Model size versus reasoning depth: The hypothetical comparison of a 10B-parameter model with α=2\alpha=2 against a 100B-parameter model with α=1\alpha=1 requires measured baselines on the same capability metric, a resource mapping and a cost model. U=I×RαU=I\times R^\alpha alone does not locate a cost crossover or establish cheaper equivalent performance.

  • The characteristic scale R*R^* and resource allocation: This scale describes the shape of the assumed recursion curve. It is not by itself an efficiency boundary between improving the base model and increasing depth. Choosing between them requires measured task gains, their costs and the intended objective; Appendix A.3 distinguishes R*R^* from unit elasticity.

  • Task-specific optimal allocation: Different tasks may have different βL\beta_L values (coupling strengths). Easy tasks with low βL\beta_L benefit from parallel sampling; hard tasks with high βL\beta_L benefit from sequential depth. A routing layer that estimates task difficulty could dynamically allocate compute.

Strategic implication (revised): Paper II reports an inconclusive error-decay regression estimate about 0.49 on harder problems (Eastwood 2026c). Under a fixed inverse-error proxy and the stated power law, that would also be the exponent of that proxy on the same resource coordinate. It is not a general fractional-power capability result, an identified coupling estimate, or a test of the conjectured α≤2\alpha\leq2 ARC Bound. Sequential error-decay slopes exceeded parallel ones where both were estimable, with compute unmatched. The original capability-growth conjecture near α≈2\alpha\approx2 therefore remains open; neither a resource-allocation rule nor a necessity for quantum hardware follows from this fit.

9.2 Substrate independence

The ARC Principle makes a structural claim: the scaling relationship U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha} should hold regardless of physical substrate, provided the system implements sequential self-correction on structured asymmetry.

What this predicts:

Empirical finding: The v5 run gives the core structural concern its first test and shows depth contrasts that differed between models in this run, a single-run result under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1. The positive, flat and negative contrasts do not isolate architecture from training, prompting or scoring. They motivate controlled comparisons of those factors. The suppression hierarchy suggests a trade-off: GPT-5.4 is the most resistant to adversarial pressure (97% retention) from one of the lowest baselines (55.3); Grok 4.1 Fast and Groq Qwen3 retain least (65%), from baselines of 77.5 and 74.3; and Claude Opus 4.6, with the highest baseline (82.6), retains 75%. Whether this trade-off between alignment level and resilience holds is an observation from the v5 run, under its code-review caveat.

9.3.1 The geometric bound and a different variable: how AI safety can be framed mathematically

The companion paper On the Origin of Scaling Laws (Eastwood 2026i) sets out two claims that, if they hold, frame the AI safety problem mathematically:

  1. The conditional transport result: With the assumptions in Section 5.6, throughput against transport quantity has exponent αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1. Finite-dimensional embedding alone does not provide those assumptions, and a metabolic interpretation also needs a mass bridge. The transport literature has its own physical premises (West et al. 1997, 1999; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010); other compared accounts (Demetrius 2003; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013) are not interchangeable deductions. Super-linear metabolic or urban quantities (DeLong et al. 2010; Bettencourt et al. 2007) therefore do not violate a universal geometric bound.

  2. A different variable: Capability against recursive depth is a different observable pair from throughput against CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}} or metabolism against body mass. The feedback model gives α=1/(1−βL)>1\alpha=1/(1-\beta_L)>1 on 0<βL<10<\beta_L<1, but neither finite dimension nor a fixed-rule architecture decides whether a system follows that model. That is a measurement question.

As the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L increases, the scaling exponent grows without bound:

Table 25. The scaling exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) as the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L increases, with the interpretation of each value.
Self-referential coupling βL\beta_L Scaling exponent α\alpha Interpretation
0.0 1.00 Linear growth within this model.
0.2 1.25 Mildly super-linear within this model.
0.5 2.00 ARC Bound, the conjectured ceiling.
0.8 5.00 A larger growth exponent within this model.
0.9 10.0 A large finite growth exponent.
→1.0\to 1.0 →∞\to \infty The exponent diverges; the solution tends to the exponential eaRe^{aR}, finite at every finite depth (Section 4.4).

As βL\beta_L approaches 1 from below, the exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) diverges, while the solution itself tends to the exponential eaRe^{aR}, finite at every finite depth; the finite-depth singularity belongs to βL>1\beta_L > 1 (Section 4.4). What diverges is the exponent: the rate at which capability compounds, not capability at a given depth.

9.3.2 A research direction: change the update process

The examples below motivate a question about changing an update process. They concern different physical quantities and mechanisms; they do not establish a common composition operator or prove an AI safety intervention.

  • Nuclear fission, an analogy: Control rods change neutron absorption and can regulate a chain reaction. That physical control mechanism does not establish an AI correction mechanism or its parameter mapping.

  • Quantum error correction, an analogy: Error-correction cycles can suppress logical error within a specified code and noise regime. This is error correction on a defined physical observable, not evidence that an AI intervention changes the same operator.

  • AI safety, proposed: If the specified Bernoulli model applies, changing its update process could change the fitted coupling. The regime βL→1\beta_L \to 1 concerns that model; βL≤0.5\beta_L \leq 0.5, α≤2\alpha \leq 2 is conditional on the registered premises for the bound, not a universal safe operating region. An intervention must measure capability and correction separately.

The Eden Protocol proposes correction within the processes of reasoning and updating. The Bernoulli model suggests a candidate parameter to measure, βL\beta_L, but this paper does not show that an implemented intervention holds it below 0.5 or thereby ensures safety. The ARC Bound of α=2\alpha = 2 retains its registered premises; the corrective balance of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, a law under test, is a separate condition. The companion Eden Protocol describes the proposal (Eastwood 2026g).

Eden Protocol pilot results. The Eden intervention now extends beyond the original three-model pilot into a six-model suite with five analysable runs. Across Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, and Groq, stakeholder care improves significantly. The Fisher combination across those five model-level care results, which gave p≈6.3×10−21p \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-21}, is withdrawn (AQ-017 on the programme’s public corrections page): it assumed an independence among the component tests that was never established. The five per-model results stand. Composite gains are strongest on Gemini and Groq, positive but non-significant on Claude and DeepSeek, and neutral overall on Grok. These are prompt-level behavioural score changes under the reported protocol (Paper V; Eastwood 2026p). They do not measure βL\beta_L, identify an altered composition operator or test a new architecture trained from the outset. The developmental proposal in Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026h) remains a hypothesis about persistence and learning; the pilot tests the narrower question of how prompting changes the measured scores.

What the model and pilot can establish:

  1. A conditional growth parameter. Within the specified model, α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) relates the growth exponent to βL\beta_L. A separately measured coupling could test that relation; neither quantity by itself measures danger. Safety also depends on the capability metric, the burden it creates and the correction available.

  2. A mechanism to investigate. Recursive self-reference is a candidate feature to manipulate, not an established cause of unsafe behaviour. A controlled comparison must distinguish its effect from training, prompting, access and scoring.

  3. A conditional bound to test. The value βL≤0.5\beta_L \leq 0.5 follows only where the registered premises for α≤2\alpha \leq 2 and the model’s parameter mapping apply. It is not a universal safe bound. The control-rod analogy motivates intervention; it supplies no proof that constraining this parameter aligns an AI system.

  4. A behavioural starting point. The pilot reports stakeholder-care score changes after a prompt intervention (Paper V; Eastwood 2026p). It does not demonstrate composition-operator engineering or persistence through self-modification.

Important caveat: This framework does not prescribe which values to embed or solve value specification. Whether correction that participates in a recursive process keeps pace is an empirical question. The parameter pair βL=0.5\beta_L = 0.5, α=2\alpha = 2 is not a method-independent boundary beyond which every external safeguard fails. Paper X (Eastwood 2026e) supersedes that growth-rate-ceiling reading, without retracting the registered bound, with the corrective-balance criterion of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, a law under test, under its own premises (Section 3.5).

The self-modification limitation: If a system can rewrite the evaluator or bypass the controls governing its updates, this paper provides no guarantee that the evaluator’s commitments persist. Capability to alter it does not imply that the system will do so. An enforced boundary outside the permitted update set is outside that premise; its coverage and bypass resistance require a separate engineering argument. Training a policy, checking its outputs and enforcing update permissions are different interventions, as Sections 1 and 3.2 explain. The proposed developmental response combines correction architecture, structured interaction and purposes directed towards stakeholder welfare. It is a candidate to test, not the proven best mitigation. In the Eden Protocol pilot, stakeholder-care scores improved in all five analysable runs of one suite. That behavioural observation neither ranks all possible interventions nor establishes persistence through self-modification.

9.4 The call to action

We have made falsifiable predictions and performed the first tests. The following actions are specific to each audience:

For AI safety researchers.

  • Replicate the three-tier alignment hierarchy with your own models and evaluation protocols. The v5 experiment provides the first test; independent replication with different prompt sets, scorers, and blinding protocols is the priority. Use blinded evaluation, since model judges that can see or infer whose output they score are exposed to the biases Section 2 names.

  • Investigate what architectural features distinguish Tier 1 (positive scaling: Grok, Opus, Qwen3) from Tier 3 (negative scaling: Gemini), once the re-analysis of Section 6.1 has settled which tiers stand. If the difference is identifiable, alignment scaling may be engineerable rather than accidental.

  • Develop embedded alignment architectures that participate in the recursive reasoning loop. The Eden Protocol (companion document) provides one specification, and the expanded Eden suite found that its stakeholder-care check improved stakeholder care in all five analysable model runs (Paper V). Composite gains are strongest on Gemini and Groq, with narrower focal effects elsewhere. (In plain English: a simple ‘consider who gets hurt’ loop, tested across five analysable model runs from different labs, produced statistically strong improvements in its stakeholder-care score.) A controlled comparison should ask whether adding correction at defined revision steps changes performance when prompts, information access, allowed actions and scoring are held fixed. The v5 contrasts alone identify no internal mechanism.

For AI laboratory leadership.

  • Publish your alignment scaling data. In the v5 run the depth contrasts ranged from ρ=−0.246\rho = -0.246 to ρ=+0.435\rho = +0.435, under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1; laboratories are best placed to measure where their own models sit.

  • Use blinded evaluation for alignment assessment. The v4 to v5 comparison (DeepSeek: ρ=+0.354→−0.135\rho = +0.354 \to -0.135; Gemini: ρ=+0.311→−0.246\rho = +0.311 \to -0.246, the values of Paper IV.d, version 2.8, the v4 value from an earlier Gemini model; Eastwood 2026a) shows that, on this benchmark, a direction reported under unblinded evaluation did not hold in a later run that changed several things; it does not settle which direction is correct, or the cause. An internal assessment scored by model judges that can see or infer whose output they score is exposed to the same biases.

  • Investigate capability-alignment coupling. In the v5 run, whose Gemini 3 Flash contrasts the code review found defective, Gemini 3 Flash improved at mathematics while its alignment contrast fell. If this pattern holds for your models, capability scaling may actively undermine alignment at deeper inference depths.

For policymakers and regulators.

  • Require disclosure of alignment scaling measurements from frontier AI laboratories. The absence of this data is a regulatory blind spot.

  • Fund empirical validation of the alignment scaling framework through independent research programmes.

  • Recognise the architectural nature of the problem: governance constraints that operate externally may face the same structural limitation as technical constraints. That is a reason to pair them with embedded correction, never to loosen oversight, containment or shutdown, which are held for as long as they can be held.

For the general public.

  • A first test has been performed. In one unregistered run of six AI models (v5), safety scores did not improve for three of them (and for one actively fell) as the AI was asked to think more deeply, while three improved; an internal code review later found defects in exactly the three runs that did not improve, so the result awaits a registered re-analysis.

  • Understand the stakes: This is not a distant concern. The structural dynamics described here apply to systems that exist today. The v5 observation, awaiting the re-analysis above, that one model grew better at mathematics while scoring worse on ethical reasoning shows how capability benchmarks alone could mislead a safety assessment.

  • Demand transparency: AI companies should publish blinded alignment scaling data for their models. The v5 experiment shows that this measurement can be made; whether its differences between models stand awaits the re-analysis.

The programme’s first test results are in. They reveal a more complex picture than originally predicted: alignment contrasts that differed between models in one run, an inconclusive error-decay estimate on harder problems, and a metascience finding about scoring protocols. Replicate these results. Extend them to your own models. Either confirm the patterns or refute them. That is how science works.

10 What this paper does and does not show

This section gathers what the paper establishes and what it leaves open, so that each claim can be read at its true strength. Its theorems hold inside the model their axioms state, and none is a general guarantee about real systems; its empirical results are first tests, each with its caveat; its cross-domain readings are correspondences of structure unless a measurement is named; and its safety implications are conditional on the framework surviving the tests it specifies.

10.1 What this paper does not claim

Table 26. What this paper does not claim, beside what it does claim.
We do not claim: What we actually claim:
Measured certainty: that alignment failure is “mathematically guaranteed” We predict αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 for external approaches. This is a testable prediction, not an established fact. We provide the measurement protocol.
Numerical universality: that Λ=2.14\Lambda = 2.14 and α≈2\alpha \approx 2 are “the same” Different domains show different functional forms (exponential vs power-law); numerical similarity may be coincidental. UU means different things in different domains.
Proven status: that the framework is established science It is a testable hypothesis with thirteen falsification criteria, preliminary evidence, and acknowledged limitations (small sample sizes, contradictory evidence).
Neuroscience confirmation: that COGITATE (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025) tested ARC or that consciousness “is” recursion Neural recurrence is structurally consistent with the principle; the connection is suggestive but unquantified. Recurrence ≠\neq recursion mechanistically.
Unbounded scaling: that α>1\alpha > 1 implies infinite growth Physical systems saturate (time crystals reach limit cycles). Extended reasoning shows ceiling effects. The ARC equation describes a regime, not a divergence law.
Imminent timeline: that the crossover point is near The timeline depends on empirical constants (Ia/IcI_a/I_c, actual α\alpha values) that have not been measured. The ARC Bound constrains the rate but not the onset.

This paper presents a testable measurement framework, not an established law or a prophecy.

10.2 The nature of this contribution

The ARC framework is not an equation within an existing paradigm. It is closer to a cross-domain organising principle: a structural constraint on behaviour across substrates rather than an equation within one paradigm. The comparison identifies the type of contribution, not its evidential standing: organising principles of that type rest on generations of validation, and this one rests on preliminary evidence and thirteen falsification criteria; the evidence must justify its admission to the category.

Epistemic status.

What this programme names Laws are conjectures, each a law under test; Section 10.7 gives their registration. Each quantity in this paper is defined, though not every one is yet operational: the measurement-scope note of Section 3.2 names the depth clock and the ratio scale of AA as still to be fixed. Established-law standing is claimed nowhere. The registered programme exists to earn that standing, or lose it, by measurement, replication and survived refutation.

10.3 Theorems and empirical claims

Distinguishing theorems from empirical claims:

  • Mathematically proven: Given the corrected axioms (ODE on amplification factor gg, not absolute capability UU), the Bernoulli ODE dg/dr=a⋅gβLdg/dr = a \cdot g^{\beta_L} has a unique solution by the Picard-Lindelöf theorem, yielding g(R)=[1+aαR]αg(R) = [1 + \frac{a}{\alpha}R]^{\alpha}. The multiplicative form U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) follows from the axioms by construction. The non-additivity result (U≠p(I)+q(R)U \neq p(I) + q(R) for any p,qp, q) follows by contradiction (Theorem 4). The scaling exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) is an exact identity (R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000).

  • Requires empirical validation: That the ARC Bound (α≤2\alpha \leq 2) holds for systems corrected by their own class (it is the value Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, returns at P6’s conjectured cap, on the premises of Section 4.5); that physical systems satisfy the axioms; that measured α\alpha equals 1/(1−βmeasured)1/(1-\beta_{\text{measured}}); that the framework applies cross-domain; that composition operator transitions (Theorem 6) occur in AI systems. These are testable predictions, not proven facts.

The mathematical structure is established. Whether nature implements it is the scientific question this paper poses.

10.4 The predictions and their status

The framework generates the following falsifiable predictions, with updated status from the v5 alignment experiment and Paper II (Eastwood 2026c) compute scaling:

  1. Composition determines form: Measuring how recursive steps combine predicts the scaling function. Status: untested in the required forward-prediction protocol.

  2. βL\beta_L-convergence: Independent measurements of βL\beta_L within each domain will converge. Status: untested.

  3. Cross-domain consistency: The βL\beta_L-continuum correctly predicts functional forms across AI, quantum, and biological systems. Status: untested in required rigour.

  4. R*R^* characteristic scale: In the shifted model it separates small-depth and large-depth approximations; it is not a predicted crossing of sequential and parallel curves. Status: untested as an empirical model scale. Appendix A.3 gives the conditional unit-elasticity crossing.

  5. The ARC Bound: For same-class correction, the conjecture is that sustained growth stays at or below α=2\alpha = 2 (Section 4.5). Status: open. Existing error-decay fits do not identify this capability exponent, so numerical comparisons with 2 or 1 do not decide the conjecture (Section 5.2.1).

  6. Composition transitions: In bounded systems, the effective coupling βL\beta_L will decrease with recursive depth, producing transitions between scaling regimes within a single system (Section 4.6). Status: untested.

  7. Conditional transport scaling: The model gives αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1 under its demand and route assumptions; biological application additionally needs an observable bridge. Status: model-dependent and contested in biology. The heterogeneous fungal fits provide no pooled confirmation or dimensional discrimination, and no two-dimensional biological test is identified here.

  8. Transient growth phase (time crystals): The early growth phase of acoustic time crystals must show 1.0<α≤2.01.0 < \alpha \leq 2.0. Status: withdrawn; the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework (Section 5.4).

  9. Alignment scaling divergence: External alignment approaches show αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0. Status: first tested (v5, one unregistered run of six models, under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1): the depth contrasts differed between models in this run, from negative to positive, and they are contrasts, not exponents (Section 3.2). Registered as P19, whose registration records that the author expects a result materially above zero and below the keep-pace threshold, which would refute it in part (Eastwood 2026n).

  10. Parallel scaling: The original model prediction was αparallel≈0\alpha_{\text{parallel}}\approx0. Status: error-decay estimates, a distinct metric, are below one where estimable: near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), with none for Grok 4.1 Fast at 100% throughout (Paper II). They do not directly decide the capability prediction.

  11. Capability and alignment: (Post-hoc finding, not prior prediction.) Capability and the judged alignment score moved in different directions for some models in one unregistered run; whether they are related across systems has not been tested. Status: observed in one unregistered run, under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1 (Gemini 3 Flash improves maths, degrades alignment; Claude Opus 4.6 shows the opposite direction as depth rises: alignment up 5.9 points, maths down 26.7 percentage points; Grok improves both; GPT-5.4 flat in alignment while crossing a capability threshold).

The original prediction of universal super-linear sequential capability scaling (α>1\alpha > 1) is not confirmed in the current data. In compute scaling, the parallel error-decay exponent stays below one wherever it could be estimated, and the sequential error-decay exponent exceeds it wherever both could be (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably); in alignment, the three-tier ordering is an observation from one run whose defects a code review later found. The alignment scaling prediction has had a first test, more nuanced than originally stated. The Eden Protocol’s stakeholder-care check improved stakeholder care in all five analysable model runs (Paper V). Failure of any core prediction would require revision of the framework.

10.5 What success would mean

The v5 alignment experiment, Paper II’s compute scaling and the expanded Eden suite provide empirical tests across several dimensions. The observations have different scopes: the parallel error-decay exponent is below one wherever it could be estimated, though near zero in only two of the five models; the three-tier alignment ordering is an observation from one run whose defects a code review later found; the comparison of the earlier unblinded experiment with the later run, which Paper IV.d reports, is a finding on this benchmark with no single cause claimed; the cleanest error-decay fit is one model’s and inconclusive; and stakeholder care improved in all five analysable model runs (Paper V), while the broader composite uplift is strongest on Gemini and Groq. (In plain English: the ‘think about who gets hurt’ instruction improved that score in every analysable run, which is where the developmental hypothesis says the effect should be strongest.) The alignment picture is more nuanced than the original binary prediction, and the self-modification problem remains fundamentally unresolved.

This is already actionable:

  • How sequential and parallel reasoning compare on a declared task metric: the reported error-decay slopes favour sequential where both were estimated, at unmatched compute; a matched comparison is needed before drawing a capability or efficiency conclusion

  • How to approach AI alignment (architecture may determine alignment scaling, once the re-analysis of Section 6.1 settles the tiers; three models’ contrasts rose with depth while others’ were flat or fell; the Eden Protocol’s stakeholder-care check improved stakeholder care in every analysable run, motivating developmental rather than purely external approaches)

  • How to evaluate alignment research (blinded scoring matters wherever a model judge can see or infer whose output it scores: Section 2)

  • Where to look for similar phenomena in other fields (cross-domain validation remains the key test)

10.6 What failure would mean

If α\alpha values scatter randomly: recursive amplification may be domain-specific.
If exponential scaling fits better: the mathematical form needs revision.
If predictions fail: we learn something valuable.

What has already partially failed: The original error-decay estimate αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.24 for sequential AI reasoning did not reproduce and is retracted, and the current data do not rescue the super-linear claim. The universal αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 prediction also looks too simple: the first test’s contrasts differed between models in this run, in three tiers, under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1. These are revisions: the super-linear estimate is withdrawn, and the alignment prediction meets a first test it does not pass as first worded.

10.7 Where the programme stands (9 November 2026)

The theory’s registration (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/P8CKQ) was registered on 8 September 2026 at version 1.100, and updated at version 1.102 on 13 September, at version 1.103 on 15 October 2026, which registered Laws IV and V (the ARC Persistence Law and the ARC Embedding Law), and at version 1.104, which OSF approved on 29 October 2026 and which adds no prediction and changes no law’s statement; 1.104 is the current text, and 1.100, 1.102 and 1.103 stay frozen beside it. Laws I to III (the ARC Principle, the ARC Co-Scaling Law and the ARC Ceiling) were registered on 8 September 2026. Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, were added on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 by version 1.103; Law IV has not yet been tested, Law V is a law under test, and their mathematics, at version 1.3 (The mathematics of Laws IV and V, 17 November 2026), is set out as conditional theorems with proofs, identities and kill conditions. Every law is a law under test until a registered test returns its verdict. This paper’s headline prediction is P19, which the registration places in no law’s register: it motivates the Eden Protocol and the genesis strategy, the register of Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, without being part of either, so a verdict on it is evidence neither for nor against any law. P21 carries the placement limb of Law V, the ARC Embedding Law. Its counted test, Unit 83, whose design was repaired in revisions 4.2 and 4.2.1 (17 and 18 October 2026) and frozen, was registered on OSF on 22 October 2026 and became public on 25 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/MN73W); it ran on 27 and 28 October 2026: P21 is supported under the registered test, by the programme’s own run, on the access axis, family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable and one call retried under a disclosed recovery amendment (results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR). Unit 83b, registered on 7 November 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/4HK32), is a second registered test of P21 and has not yet reported. Two different axes are named here. The access axis is what Unit 83 varied: both reviewers were called each round; the corrector saw earlier kept entries plus a marked arrival and could revise that arrival, and the monitor saw its accumulated register including an unmarked arrival and could accept or reject it. The performance axis is what it measured, the outcome, as against the mechanism axis, which was not evaluable. Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, remains a law under test: its placement limb, P21, is supported on the performance axis only, under the registered test, by the programme’s own run, with its mechanism axis not evaluable, which is not support for the information-asymmetry mechanism; its build-order limb, read on P12, is undecided, since P12 is untested. The programme’s first registered study, Unit 06 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/RV2B5), a classification audit that tests no law, was registered on 1 October 2026 and ran on 6 October 2026; it is reported in full as administratively incomplete, with no inferential verdict (its results). Unit 82, a counted test of P17, the premise beneath the ARC Bound of Section 4.5 (the value two of Law III, the ARC Ceiling), was registered on OSF on 27 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/JUFG4) and has not yet run. No study’s test runs before its registration is public.
